Its new significance is veterinary: laboratory ferret studies showed subcutaneous flubendazole disrupts embryo development inside female Dracunculus medinensis so larvae cannot infect copepods, and a 2019 randomised field trial in 23 Chadian villages (600 dogs) followed for 33 months found that villages receiving flubendazole together with proactive dog tethering had 83% fewer emerging dog worms than villages under baseline measures. A second, larger field trial ("Flubendazole 2.0") was designed to confirm the effect. If confirmed, this would be the first therapeutic tool the eradication programme has ever had against the dog reservoir.
Sources: ChEMBL — flubendazole (CHEMBL1454946) <https://www.ebi.ac.uk/chembl/explore/compound/CHEMBL1454946>; Cleveland et al. — flubendazole trials in ferrets and dogs in Chad (2022) <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9128682>; Dupper et al. — flubendazole plus tethering in dogs, Chad (2026) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41628272>

### Fosravuconazole
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/fosravuconazole/
TL;DR: The first drug tested against fungal mycetoma in a randomised trial — safe and once-weekly, but it did not beat itraconazole.
Summary: Fosravuconazole is a triazole antifungal designed for onychomycosis and repurposed for eumycetoma. In the first randomised, double-blind clinical trial for the disease, run at a single centre in Sudan by the Mycetoma Research Centre with DNDi and Eisai, it was compared at two once-weekly doses against daily itraconazole, with surgery at six months. Neither dose was superior to itraconazole, and both had numerically lower efficacy — but fosravuconazole showed no new safety concerns and its once-weekly dosing is far easier for patients who travel long distances to a clinic. That combination of a negative efficacy result and a real practical advantage is the honest outcome of the trial.
Sources: First randomised mycetoma trial results (The Lancet Infectious Diseases) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39098321/>; A balancing act: the pioneering mycetoma trial in Sudan (PLOS NTD) <https://journals.plos.org/plosntds/article?id=10.1371/journal.pntd.0013000>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Ganaplacide (KAF156, in GanLum)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/ganaplacide/
TL;DR: The first new-acting malaria drug to clear Phase 3 since 1999 — once-daily granules, 97.4% efficacy.
Summary: Ganaplacide is an imidazolopiperazine found in a 2.3-million-molecule Novartis screen, disrupting the parasite's internal protein secretory pathway (resistance markers in CARL and transporter genes, not kelch13). In GanLum — paired with once-daily lumefantrine as three days of granules — the KALUMA Phase 3 (1,688 patients, 34 sites, 12 African countries) met non-inferiority against Coartem at 97.4% PCR-corrected efficacy, with transmission-blocking activity. Novartis seeks approvals; if granted, this is the first novel malaria treatment in a quarter-century and the designated answer to artemisinin partial resistance.
Sources: Novartis — KALUMA Phase 3 meets endpoint (Nov 2025) <https://www.novartis.com/news/media-releases/novartis-phase-iii-trial-next-generation-malaria-treatment-klu156-ganlum-meets-primary-endpoint-potential-combat-antimalarial-resistance>; MMV — GanLum pipeline <https://www.mmv.org/mmv-pipeline-antimalarial-drugs/ganaplacide-lumefantrine>

### IID432
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/iid432/
TL;DR: A cyanotriazole inhibitor of the Chagas parasite's topoisomerase II that delivered a single-dose sterile cure in a chronic mouse model.
Summary: IID432 is a Novartis cyanotriazole optimised for Chagas disease from a phenotypic kinetoplastid screen. It covalently engages a parasite-specific cysteine (Cys477) of T. cruzi topoisomerase II, trapping the enzyme on DNA while sparing the human TOP2A, with an EC50 of 8 nM. In a bioluminescent chronic mouse model a single oral dose of 25 mg/kg achieved sterile cure with no recrudescence after cyclophosphamide immunosuppression — reported as the first single-dose cure in a chronic T. cruzi model. Medicinal-chemistry optimisation removed the first-generation liabilities (lymphopenia, neutrophilia from sphingolipid-pathway modulation). It remains preclinical, but it is the most advanced new-chemical-class candidate behind AN2-502998.
Sources: Discovery of IID432 for Chagas disease (J Med Chem 2026) <https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jmedchem.5c02459>; IID432 single-dose clearance in chronic Chagas model (PNAS 2026) <https://researchonline.lshtm.ac.uk/id/eprint/4683118/>

### Inmazeb (atoltivimab + maftivimab + odesivimab)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/inmazeb/
TL;DR: A three-antibody cocktail that was the first treatment ever approved for Ebola — shown superior to ZMapp and remdesivir in the PALM trial.
Summary: Inmazeb (REGN-EB3) combines three fully human monoclonal antibodies that bind non-overlapping regions of the Zaire ebolavirus glycoprotein, so a single escape mutation cannot defeat it. In the 681-patient PALM randomised trial during the 2018–2020 DRC outbreak it reduced mortality more than ZMapp or remdesivir, with the clearest benefit when given early, and the trial was stopped early for superiority. The US FDA approved it on 14 October 2020 — the first approval of any Ebola treatment — for adults and children including neonates born to positive mothers, and BARDA contracted a six-year supply for the US stockpile. WHO strongly recommends Inmazeb or ansuvimab for confirmed Zaire ebolavirus disease. Like ansuvimab it covers only Zaire ebolavirus, not Sudan or Bundibugyo virus.
Sources: Regeneron — FDA approval of Inmazeb (Oct 2020) <https://investor.regeneron.com/node/24386/pdf>; Markham — REGN-EB3 first approval (2021) <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7799152>; ChEMBL — atoltivimab <https://www.ebi.ac.uk/chembl/explore/compound/CHEMBL4298183>

### Isoniazid
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/isoniazid/
TL;DR: One of the four drugs in standard tuberculosis treatment, and the mainstay of preventive treatment for people at high risk.
Summary: Isoniazid has been a cornerstone of tuberculosis treatment since 1952 and is unusual in being highly specific to mycobacteria, which is why it is well tolerated. It kills actively dividing bacteria and is the drug most used for preventive treatment in people with latent infection — a single drug taken for months to stop the disease developing. Resistance, common in multidrug-resistant strains, is detected through mutations in the katG and inhA genes.
Sources: WHO — tuberculosis (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/tuberculosis>; WHO — Global tuberculosis report 2024 <https://www.who.int/teams/global-programme-on-tuberculosis-and-lung-health/tb-reports/global-tuberculosis-report-2024>

### Itraconazole
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/itraconazole/
TL;DR: The azole antifungal that is the standard of care for eumycetoma — taken for months to years, and the benchmark every new candidate is measured against.
Summary: Itraconazole is the mainstay of medical treatment for eumycetoma, usually combined with surgery, and is also used for other deep and implantation mycoses. It inhibits fungal cytochrome P450 14α-demethylase (CYP51), blocking ergosterol synthesis in the cell membrane. For mycetoma it must be taken for a year or more at 400 mg daily, and even then cure is not guaranteed — in the only randomised trial ever run in the disease, 75% of patients on itraconazole plus surgery were cured at 12 months. Its limitations are the reason the field keeps looking: a long course, drug-drug interactions, cost and variable access in the endemic countries where it is most needed. WHO lists it among essential medicines, but in practice availability and price remain barriers.
Sources: Fahal et al. — fosravuconazole versus itraconazole, Lancet Infect Dis 2024 <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39098321/>; WHO — mycetoma (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mycetoma>

### Ivermectin
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/ivermectin/
TL;DR: A once-a-year tablet that transformed river blindness and lymphatic filariasis, and is donated free for as long as it is needed.
Summary: Ivermectin paralyses parasitic worms by opening glutamate-gated chloride channels that vertebrates do not have, which is why it is so safe. A single dose suppresses microfilariae for months, and repeated annual mass treatment broke transmission of river blindness across much of Africa and Latin America. Merck has donated it free for onchocerciasis and lymphatic filariasis since 1987, making it one of the largest drug donation programmes in history. It is also a treatment for scabies and strongyloidiasis.
Sources: WHO — onchocerciasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/onchocerciasis>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Ixchiq (chikungunya vaccine)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/ixchiq/
TL;DR: The first licensed chikungunya vaccine, whose US licence was suspended in 2025 and withdrawn in 2026 after chikungunya-like serious events — while Brazil rolls it out.
Summary: Ixchiq is a live-attenuated chikungunya vaccine and the first product of any kind licensed against the disease, given as a single dose. In May 2025 the FDA and CDC paused its use in people aged 60 and older after post-marketing reports of serious neurological and cardiac events — seventeen in total, including two deaths, in recipients aged 62 to 89. In August 2025 the FDA suspended the US biologics licence over chikungunya-like illness in recipients, including hospitalisations and encephalitis with one death, and in January 2026 Valneva voluntarily withdrew the US application. Europe lifted its own elderly restriction, and the product's centre of gravity moved to endemic countries: Brazil licensed it in April 2025, approved locally made VLA1555 in May 2026, and launched a pilot Ixchiq campaign in February 2026 with about 45,000 vaccinated. Four-year follow-up shows 95% seroresponse after a single shot.
Sources: FDA — Ixchiq licence suspension (Aug 2025) <https://www.fda.gov/safety/medical-product-safety-information/fda-update-safety-ixchiq-chikungunya-vaccine-live-fda-suspends-biologics-license-fda-safety>; Valneva — US withdrawal (Jan 2026) <https://valneva.com/press-release/valneva-provides-update-on-chikungunya-vaccine-ixchiq/>

### Linezolid
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/linezolid/
TL;DR: An oxazolidinone antibiotic that is effective against resistant tuberculosis, and also active against the leprosy bacillus.
Summary: Linezolid blocks the bacterial ribosome and is one of the most effective drugs in the BPaLM regimen for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. Its problem is toxicity: prolonged use causes bone-marrow suppression, peripheral neuropathy and optic nerve damage, so it needs monitoring and patients often need dose adjustment. It illustrates the trade-off in resistant tuberculosis, where effective drugs are scarce enough that toxicity is accepted as the price of a cure.
Sources: WHO — Global tuberculosis report 2024 <https://www.who.int/teams/global-programme-on-tuberculosis-and-lung-health/tb-reports/global-tuberculosis-report-2024>; WHO — tuberculosis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/tuberculosis>

### Liposomal amphotericin B
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/liposomal-amphotericin-b/
TL;DR: A single-dose infusion that cures visceral leishmaniasis in South Asia, and the most effective treatment for it.
Summary: Liposomal amphotericin B packages the antifungal amphotericin B in fat spheres that concentrate in the organs where Leishmania lives, killing the parasite while reducing the kidney toxicity of the free drug. In South Asia a single dose can cure visceral leishmaniasis, which transformed treatment from weeks of injections to one visit. Its limits are cost, the need for a cold chain and infusion equipment, and the logistics of supporting it — which is why combination regimens have been explored to stretch supply.
Sources: WHO — leishmaniasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leishmaniasis>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### LXE408
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/lxe408/
TL;DR: A novel oral drug for visceral leishmaniasis, developed with Novartis, that could remove injections from treatment entirely.
Summary: LXE408 is a first-in-class oral compound developed by DNDi with Novartis as a potential new treatment for visceral leishmaniasis. It is a parasite-selective inhibitor of the kinetoplastid proteasome — a mechanism new to leishmaniasis, and one active against L. donovani, L. infantum and the trypanosomes that cause Chagas disease and sleeping sickness. Two Phase II studies ran in parallel, in India and in Ethiopia, comparing LXE408 with local standard of care; recruitment and follow-up completed in 2025 and results are expected in 2026. It is the field's best hope of a short oral regimen, and it belongs to a class new to leishmaniasis, which also makes it useful if resistance to current drugs emerges. A Phase II study in cutaneous leishmaniasis in the Americas began in 2026.
Sources: DNDi — LXE408 with Novartis for visceral leishmaniasis <https://dndi.org/research-development/portfolio/lxe408-novartis-visceral-leishmaniasis/>; DNDi — LXE408 Phase 2 protocol synopsis (India) <https://dndi.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/DNDi-LXE408-01-VL-Clinical-Trial-Protocol-Synopsis.pdf>; LXE408 Ethiopia Phase II (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05957978) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05957978>; WHO — leishmaniasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leishmaniasis>

### Mebendazole
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/mebendazole/
TL;DR: A chewable deworming tablet used in school programmes against roundworm, whipworm and hookworm.
Summary: Mebendazole is the other main benzimidazole dewormer alongside albendazole, donated by Johnson & Johnson for soil-transmitted helminth control. Chewable formulations make it practical for young children, and it is a mainstay of school-based deworming, which reduces anaemia and improves growth and school attendance at very low cost.
Sources: WHO — deworming <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/soil-transmitted-helminth-infections>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Melarsoprol
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/melarsoprol/
TL;DR: An arsenic-based treatment for late-stage sleeping sickness that is effective but can itself be lethal.
Summary: Melarsoprol has been the mainstay for late-stage sleeping sickness for decades, and it is still needed for Rhodesiense disease that has reached the brain. It is an arsenic compound given by intravenous injection, and it causes a fatal post-treatment encephalopathy in a small proportion of patients — a risk that made a safer alternative urgent and drove the development of NECT, fexinidazole and acoziborole.
Sources: WHO — human African trypanosomiasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/trypanosomiasis-human-african-(sleeping-sickness)>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Miltefosine
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/miltefosine/
TL;DR: The first oral treatment for visceral leishmaniasis, but its long course and teratogenicity limit its use.
Summary: Miltefosine is an oral alkylphosphocholine that kills Leishmania by disrupting its membrane and metabolism. It was a major advance as an oral drug for visceral leishmaniasis, especially in South Asia, and is also used for cutaneous disease. Its drawbacks are a 28-day course, gastrointestinal side effects, teratogenicity (so pregnancy must be excluded and prevented), and declining efficacy in South Asia, likely from resistance.
Sources: WHO — leishmaniasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leishmaniasis>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Mosnodenvir (JNJ-1802)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/mosnodenvir/
TL;DR: A dengue antiviral with published NEJM challenge-trial protection, orphaned by J&J's exit — awaiting a new sponsor.
Summary: Mosnodenvir is a small-molecule antiviral blocking the dengue NS3–NS4B interaction (EC50 0.057–11 nM across serotypes) with, unusually for the field, demonstrated protection in a controlled human infection model: 6 of 10 high-dose recipients uninfected, the rest low-viraemia (NEJM). It was safe and well tolerated in Phase 1 and 2a. In October 2024 J&J halted the ~1,600-participant Phase 2 field study on exiting infectious diseases entirely — a commercial decision, not a safety signal — and the compound sits in limbo with adoption talks under way. The result is that dengue still has no approved antiviral, but for the first time the field holds published human efficacy data and a rescue conversation rather than just a discontinued programme.
Sources: Daily mosnodenvir as dengue prophylaxis (NEJM) <https://www.nejm.org/do/10.1056/NEJMdo008250/full>; Johnson & Johnson — discontinuation of the Phase 2 dengue study <https://www.jnj.com/media-center/press-releases/johnson-johnson-to-discontinue-phase-2-field-study-evaluating-investigational-antiviral-for-the-prevention-of-dengue>; WHO — dengue and severe dengue (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/dengue-and-severe-dengue>

### Moxidectin
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/moxidectin/
TL;DR: A longer-acting relative of ivermectin, approved in 2018 for river blindness, that suppresses microfilariae for longer.
Summary: Moxidectin is a macrocyclic lactone that works on the same glutamate-gated chloride channel as ivermectin but stays in the body longer, so a single dose suppresses onchocercal microfilariae for a full year or more. The FDA approved it for onchocerciasis in 2018 on the basis of a trial showing better and more sustained skin microfilarial suppression than ivermectin. It has not yet displaced ivermectin in mass programmes, where the free donation of ivermectin is decisive.
Sources: WHO — onchocerciasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/onchocerciasis>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Moxifloxacin
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/moxifloxacin/
TL;DR: The fluoroquinolone WHO names as the alternative to clarithromycin in Buruli ulcer treatment, and a repurposing candidate in its own right.
Summary: Moxifloxacin is a fluoroquinolone that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. WHO's Buruli ulcer guidance gives an eight-week course of rifampicin plus moxifloxacin as the alternative when clarithromycin cannot be used, for example in pregnancy or with macrolide intolerance. It is also a component of the BPaLM regimen for drug-resistant tuberculosis, and a 2025 study found that moxifloxacin had one of the higher maximum-kill effects against M. ulcerans among eight drugs tested, alone and in combination — which makes it both a fallback and a candidate for shorter regimens.
Sources: WHO — Treatment of Mycobacterium ulcerans disease: guidance for health workers (2012) <https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/77771>; Antimicrob Agents Chemother — repurposing drugs for Buruli ulcer (2025) <https://doi.org/10.1128/aac.00029-25>; ChEMBL — moxifloxacin (CHEMBL32) <https://www.ebi.ac.uk/chembl/compound_report_card/CHEMBL32/>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Nifurtimox
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/nifurtimox/
TL;DR: A Chagas and sleeping-sickness drug; as part of NECT it made late-stage sleeping sickness far easier to treat.
Summary: Nifurtimox is a nitrofuran active against both Trypanosoma cruzi and T. brucei. It is a second-line option for Chagas disease (a 60–90-day course with significant side effects), but its landmark role is in NECT — nifurtimox-eflornithine combination therapy — which replaced weeks of melarsoprol infusions for late-stage sleeping sickness with a simpler, safer regimen. It is on the WHO essential medicines list.
Sources: DNDi — sleeping sickness <https://dndi.org/diseases/sleeping-sickness/>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Nitazoxanide (as a fascioliasis alternative)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/nitazoxanide/
TL;DR: The only plausible alternative to triclabendazole for fascioliasis, and a poor one — cure rates around 30% in the patients who need it most.
Summary: Nitazoxanide is a broad-spectrum antiparasitic used for intestinal infections, and it has been tested as a fallback for fascioliasis when triclabendazole fails. The evidence is discouraging: in an Egyptian series of patients who had already failed two doses of triclabendazole, nitazoxanide cured about 30%; in a Peruvian case series it was ineffective. It is included here because it defines the problem rather than solving it — triclabendazole is the only recommended medicine for human fascioliasis, resistance is emerging, and there is no established alternative behind it.
Sources: Triclabendazole treatment failure for Fasciola hepatica (EID) <https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/27/7/20-3900_article>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Olorofim
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/olorofim/
TL;DR: A new antifungal from the tuberculosis-style pipeline that has excellent activity against the main mycetoma fungus in the laboratory.
Summary: Olorofim is an orotomide antifungal that inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase and is in development for multidrug-resistant mould infections. It has shown excellent in vitro activity against Madurella mycetomatis, the main cause of eumycetoma, which makes it one of the most promising compounds for a disease with no reliably effective drug. It is not being developed for mycetoma — the market cannot support it — so the field's route is to follow the antifungal pipeline and find funding to test such compounds where the disease occurs.
Sources: The antifungal pipeline — fosmanogepix, ibrexafungerp, olorofim <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8501344/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Oxamniquine
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/oxamniquine/
TL;DR: An older drug that worked only against Schistosoma mansoni and has largely been abandoned.
Summary: Oxamniquine was developed as a schistosomiasis treatment but is active only against Schistosoma mansoni. It fell out of use because praziquantel covers all three main schistosome species in a single dose and was easier to supply. Its story is a warning about reliance on a single drug: when the only remaining medicine fails, the alternatives have already been retired.
Sources: WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>; WHO — schistosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/schistosomiasis>

### Oxfendazole
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/oxfendazole/
TL;DR: A veterinary dewormer being developed as a treatment that could kill the adult worms of river blindness, lymphatic filariasis and loiasis.
Summary: Oxfendazole is a benzimidazole used for decades in animals, now in clinical development for human filarial disease by DNDi and partners. What makes it interesting is the possibility of macrofilaricidal activity — killing adult worms rather than only suppressing their offspring — which would shorten elimination programmes that currently must run for the 10–15 year lifespan of the adult parasite, and would treat the patient rather than only the community. Phase II work is running across several infections: the eWHORM partnership's basket trial in Africa, where trichuriasis recruitment is complete and onchocerciasis and loiasis sites have opened, and a Phase IIa proof-of-concept trial for lymphatic filariasis started in India by the ICMR in 2025. A commercialisable tablet formulation is in development.
Sources: DNDi — oxfendazole <https://dndi.org/research-development/portfolio/oxfendazole/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Paromomycin
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/paromomycin/
TL;DR: An injectable antibiotic that kills Leishmania and is used, often in combination, for visceral leishmaniasis.
Summary: Paromomycin is an aminoglycoside that disrupts the parasite's ribosomes and mitochondria. Given intramuscularly for 21 days it cures visceral leishmaniasis, and in combination with liposomal amphotericin B or miltefosine it shortens and cheapens treatment. It is also used topically for some cutaneous forms. Its main limitations are injection-site pain and the need for daily injections over weeks.
Sources: WHO — leishmaniasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leishmaniasis>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Pentamidine
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/pentamidine/
TL;DR: An old injected drug for early-stage sleeping sickness, and still a first-line option there.
Summary: Pentamidine is used for the first stage of Gambiense sleeping sickness, before the parasite reaches the brain. It is given by intramuscular injection over about a week. Its limitations — injections, and poor efficacy once the parasite is in the central nervous system — are why oral treatments such as fexinidazole and acoziborole matter so much.
Sources: WHO — human African trypanosomiasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/trypanosomiasis-human-african-(sleeping-sickness)>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Pentavalent antimonials
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/antimonials/
TL;DR: The original leishmaniasis drugs — cheap and effective, but toxic to the heart and now failing in South Asia.
Summary: Sodium stibogluconate and meglumine antimoniate have treated leishmaniasis for over seventy years. They remain widely used for cutaneous disease and in some regions for visceral disease, because they are cheap. Their problems are a long course of painful injections and serious toxicity, including heart-rhythm disturbance and pancreatitis, plus widespread treatment failure in Bihar, India, where resistance became so common that antimonials were abandoned there.
Sources: WHO — leishmaniasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leishmaniasis>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Permethrin
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/permethrin/
TL;DR: A topical insecticide cream that kills scabies mites, and the same chemical class used to treat bed nets.
Summary: Permethrin is a synthetic pyrethroid. As a 5% cream washed off after 8–14 hours it kills scabies mites, and it is the first-line topical treatment for ordinary scabies. It is also applied to clothing and bed nets as an insecticide. For crusted scabies and for whole-community treatment, oral ivermectin is often preferred because topical treatment of a whole household or village is impractical.
Sources: WHO — scabies <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/scabies>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Praziquantel
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/praziquantel/
TL;DR: A single-dose tablet that kills adult schistosomes and tapeworms, and the only drug used at scale against schistosomiasis.
Summary: Praziquantel is the backbone of schistosomiasis treatment worldwide. A single oral dose kills adult worms by opening a calcium-permeable ion channel, causing paralysis and damage to the worm's surface. It is cheap, safe and on the WHO essential medicines list. Its weaknesses are that it works poorly against immature worms, requires repeated treatment to prevent reinfection, and is the only option — which makes resistance a serious concern if it emerges.
Sources: WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>; WHO — schistosomiasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/schistosomiasis>

### Pretomanid
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/pretomanid/
TL;DR: One of the three drugs in the six-month, injection-free regimen that transformed treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis.
Summary: Pretomanid is a nitroimidazole that, like delamanid, is activated by the mycobacterial enzyme Ddn. Given with bedaquiline and linezolid — the BPaLM regimen — it allows multidrug-resistant tuberculosis to be cured in six months without injections, replacing regimens that took up to two years and included injectable drugs with severe toxicity. It is one of the clearest recent gains in tuberculosis care, and it exists because of a non-profit drug developer working where the market did not.
Sources: WHO — Global tuberculosis report 2024 <https://www.who.int/teams/global-programme-on-tuberculosis-and-lung-health/tb-reports/global-tuberculosis-report-2024>; WHO — tuberculosis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/tuberculosis>

### Primaquine
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/primaquine/
TL;DR: The drug that clears the dormant liver stages of vivax malaria and blocks transmission — with one dangerous exception, G6PD deficiency.
Summary: Primaquine has two distinct jobs: it kills the hypnozoites, the dormant liver forms that cause relapses in Plasmodium vivax and P. ovale malaria, and it kills the mature gametocytes that transmit the parasite to mosquitoes. It is the only widely available drug that does the first. Its danger is that it causes haemolysis in people with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, a common genetic condition in malaria-endemic countries, so testing is recommended before use — which is itself a barrier where laboratory capacity is thin.
Sources: WHO — guidelines for malaria <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/guidelines-for-malaria>; WHO — malaria (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/malaria>

### Pyrazinamide
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/pyrazinamide/
TL;DR: The drug that shortened tuberculosis treatment from nine months to six — and whose mechanism took decades to explain.
Summary: Pyrazinamide is a prodrug that is only active in acidic conditions, which is why it works against bacteria in inflamed tissue that other drugs reach poorly. Adding it to the regimen in the 1970s shortened treatment from nine months to six, one of the largest single gains in tuberculosis care. Its mechanism was settled only recently, and it remains central to both drug-susceptible and newer resistant-disease regimens.
Sources: WHO — tuberculosis (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/tuberculosis>; WHO — Global tuberculosis report 2024 <https://www.who.int/teams/global-programme-on-tuberculosis-and-lung-health/tb-reports/global-tuberculosis-report-2024>

### Qdenga (TAK-003)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/qdenga/
TL;DR: The two-dose dengue vaccine for 6–16-year-olds in high-transmission settings — still the only WHO-recommended one.
Summary: Qdenga is a live-attenuated tetravalent dengue vaccine given in two doses three months apart, licensed in 40+ countries including Argentina, Brazil, Indonesia and Thailand. WHO's May 2024 position paper recommends it for children aged 6–16 in high-transmission settings — explicitly not younger children or low-transmission settings until DENV-3/DENV-4 protection in seronegatives is clarified. It remains the only WHO-recommended dengue vaccine after Butantan-DV's 2026 suspension, which makes resolving its serotype gaps the field's most urgent vaccine question.
Sources: WHO — dengue vaccine position paper (2024) <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240091078>; CDC — dengue vaccines (2026) <https://www.cdc.gov/dengue/hcp/vaccine/index.html>

### Rabies monoclonal antibodies
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/rabies-monoclonal-antibodies/
TL;DR: Engineered antibodies that replace scarce, plasma-derived rabies immunoglobulin — the fix for the treatment pathway's most stubborn bottleneck.
Summary: For category III exposures — transdermal bites, mucous-membrane contact or bat exposure — post-exposure prophylaxis needs antibodies as well as vaccine, to neutralise the virus before it reaches the nervous system. The standard product is human rabies immunoglobulin (RIG), derived from the plasma of vaccinated donors: expensive, in chronic global shortage, and frequently unavailable at the clinic where the bite is treated. Monoclonal antibodies (RmAb) against the rabies glycoprotein are produced at scale and consistently, without plasma, and two are licensed in India. A 2025 phase 4 study reported outcomes for a monoclonal in category III exposures, and cocktails are being evaluated where immunoglobulin cannot be obtained. WHO's 2026 fact sheet lists RmAb alongside RIG as an indicated option, and the remaining barriers are price, regional coverage of rabies virus variants, and adoption into national guidelines.
Sources: WHO — rabies (fact sheet, 17 September 2026) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/rabies>; Lancet — rabies monoclonal antibody PEP (2025) <https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(25)00735-4/fulltext>

### Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/rabies-postexposure-prophylaxis/
TL;DR: Wound washing plus a course of rabies vaccine, with immunoglobulin for severe bites — it prevents the disease completely if given in time.
Summary: Rabies PEP is the combination of immediate wound washing, a series of rabies vaccine doses, and — for category III exposures — rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into the wound. Given promptly after a bite it prevents disease essentially every time. The global problem is access: deaths happen where vaccine and immunoglobulin are unavailable, unaffordable or require travel that victims cannot make in time. Intradermal dose-sparing regimens and monoclonal antibodies are ways to stretch scarce supplies.
Sources: WHO — rabies <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/rabies>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Rifampicin
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/rifampicin/
TL;DR: The most important drug in leprosy and Buruli ulcer treatment, and the one that makes single-dose prevention possible.
Summary: Rifampicin kills mycobacteria by blocking RNA polymerase. It is the key bactericidal component of leprosy multidrug therapy, part of the antibiotic combination that cures Buruli ulcer, and the basis of single-dose post-exposure prophylaxis for contacts of leprosy patients. Because it is also a first-line tuberculosis drug, rifampicin resistance in either disease is a shared threat and its use is carefully stewarded.
Sources: WHO — leprosy <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leprosy>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Snake antivenom
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/snake-antivenom/
TL;DR: Antibodies from hyper-immunised animals that neutralise venom — the only specific treatment for snakebite, and often in short supply.
Summary: Snake antivenom is made by immunising horses or sheep with venom and harvesting the antibodies, which are then given intravenously to neutralise circulating venom. It must match the snakes of the region, so a shortage in one country cannot be filled from another's stock. Problems include cost, cold-chain requirements, a risk of allergic reactions, and a long history of poor-quality products; WHO maintains a list of prequalified antivenoms to address the last of these.
Sources: WHO — snakebite envenoming <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/snakebite-envenoming>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Suramin
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/suramin/
TL;DR: An injected drug for first-stage Rhodesiense sleeping sickness, the form of the disease that kills within weeks.
Summary: Suramin treats the early stage of Rhodesiense sleeping sickness, which is acute and must be treated urgently. It is given by intravenous injection after a test dose, because of a risk of immediate reactions. It does not cross into the brain, so late-stage disease needs a different drug — historically melarsoprol.
Sources: WHO — human African trypanosomiasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/trypanosomiasis-human-african-(sleeping-sickness)>; WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>

### Tafenoquine
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/tafenoquine/
TL;DR: A single-dose alternative to primaquine for radical cure of vivax malaria, but with the same G6PD danger.
Summary: Tafenoquine does what primaquine does — clearing dormant liver stages of Plasmodium vivax — but in a single dose rather than a 5 to 14 day course, which matters enormously for adherence in people who feel well after their fever has gone. It shares primaquine's contraindication in G6PD deficiency and therefore requires a quantitative G6PD test before use, making the diagnostic a prerequisite for the drug.
Sources: WHO — guidelines for malaria <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/guidelines-for-malaria>; WHO — malaria (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/malaria>

### Telacebec (Q203)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/telacebec/
TL;DR: A tuberculosis drug with exceptional potency against the Buruli ulcer bacterium, in trials that could shorten treatment from eight weeks to a few doses.
Summary: Telacebec is an imidazopyridine developed for tuberculosis that blocks QcrB in the mycobacterial respiratory chain. Against Mycobacterium ulcerans it has the lowest minimum inhibitory concentration of any drug tested — 0.0000075 mg/L, against 0.5 mg/L for both rifampicin and clarithromycin in a 2025 head-to-head comparison — and in mouse models it sterilised the infection after only sixteen doses, which would translate into an ultrashort regimen. The Phase 2 TREAT-BU trial began in Australia in July 2024, sponsored by Barwon Health with TB Alliance as collaborator. It is the clearest example in the NTD field of the repurposing strategy: take a molecule whose safety is already established for one mycobacterial disease and prove it works for another, rather than inventing a new drug for a market that cannot pay.
Sources: TB Alliance — telacebec trial in Buruli ulcer <https://www.tballiance.org/news-new-clinical-trial-examines-use-novel-compound-telacebec-buruli-ulcer-patients/>; TREAT-BU trial (ClinicalTrials.gov) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06481163>; PLoS NTD — regimens sterilising mice after 16 doses (2020) <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pntd.0007857>; Antimicrob Agents Chemother — repurposing drugs for Buruli ulcer (2025) <https://doi.org/10.1128/aac.00029-25>; ChEMBL — telacebec (CHEMBL3298910) <https://www.ebi.ac.uk/chembl/compound_report_card/CHEMBL3298910/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Tribendimidine
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/tribendimidine/
TL;DR: A deworming drug developed in China that is active against gut worms, including some that resist the standard drugs.
Summary: Tribendimidine is a broad-spectrum anthelmintic developed in China and used there for years. Trials have shown good activity against Ascaris, hookworm and Trichuris, and it appears effective against some benzimidazole-resistant worms, making it a candidate for combination or rotation where resistance bites. It acts on nematode nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
Sources: WHO — soil-transmitted helminths <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/soil-transmitted-helminth-infections>; WHO — soil-transmitted helminthiases (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/soil-transmitted-helminthiases>

### Triclabendazole
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/triclabendazole/
TL;DR: A deworming tablet particularly effective against liver flukes, used for fascioliasis and paragonimiasis.
Summary: Triclabendazole is a benzimidazole that is unusually active against the liver fluke Fasciola, killing both immature and adult worms, and it also treats Paragonimus lung flukes. It is on the WHO essential medicines list and was added to WHO's donated-donation programme for foodborne trematodiases. As with other benzimidazoles, its target is parasite beta-tubulin.
Sources: WHO Model List of Essential Medicines <https://list.essentialmeds.org/>; WHO — foodborne trematode infections <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/foodborne-trematode-infections>

### Vimkunya (chikungunya vaccine)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/drugs/vimkunya/
TL;DR: A virus-like-particle chikungunya vaccine approved in the US, EU, UK and Switzerland by 2026 — the product the field now leans on.
Summary: Vimkunya is a virus-like-particle vaccine against chikungunya, given as a single adjuvanted dose. Because it carries no viral genetic material it cannot cause disease, so it was never caught by the safety action that ended Ixchiq in the United States. By April 2026 it held approvals in the US (Feb 2025), EU, UK (May 2025) and Switzerland (Apr 2026, ages 12+), with Brazil (Eurofarma, Anvisa filing July 2026) and Canada pending. Published data show cross-neutralisation across CHIKV lineages after a single dose, a dedicated over-65 Phase 3, and a paediatric Phase 3 (ages 2–11) under way — the age expansion Ixchiq lost.
Sources: Vaccine — Vimkunya cross-neutralisation after a single dose (2026) <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.128892>; Bavarian Nordic — Swissmedic approval (Apr 2026) <https://www.bavarian-nordic.com/investor/news/news.aspx?news=7492>


## Diagnostics

### (1,3)-β-D-glucan serum monitoring
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/beta-d-glucan-treatment-monitoring/
TL;DR: A panfungal blood marker being tested as a way to tell whether eumycetoma treatment is working — a test the disease has never had.
Summary: (1,3)-β-D-glucan is a cell-wall component released by many fungi, including Madurella mycetomatis, and can be measured in serum. In a 2024 study of 104 patients receiving itraconazole or fosravuconazole in Sudan, serial β-D-glucan concentrations were measured over treatment to see whether they tracked clinical outcome — an attempt to give mycetoma a treatment-monitoring biomarker. The need is acute: cure is currently judged only by the slow disappearance of a mass and sinuses over a year, so neither patient nor clinician can tell early whether a painful, expensive regimen is working. A reliable biomarker would let ineffective treatment be changed sooner and shorter courses be tested.
Sources: Nyuykonge et al. — β-D-glucan to monitor azole therapy in eumycetoma (Mycoses 2024) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37872649/>

### Antibody rapid diagnostic tests
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/antibody-rdt/
TL;DR: Finger-prick strip tests that detect the body's antibody response, widely used to map who has been exposed to an NTD.
Summary: Antibody RDTs are the workhorse of NTD mapping: they are cheap, need no laboratory and are used to survey whole villages for exposure to lymphatic filariasis, onchocerciasis and other infections. Their fundamental limitation is the antibody response itself — it persists after infection clears, so a positive result indicates exposure, not necessarily active infection, and cannot be used to decide whether someone needs treatment. A newer generation of tests targets parasite antigens instead.
Sources: FIND — diagnostics for neglected diseases <https://www.finddx.org/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>; FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>

### Brugia Test Plus (BT+)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/brugia-test-plus/
TL;DR: A second-generation rapid test for the Brugia species that the standard filariasis antigen test cannot detect.
Summary: Brugia malayi and B. timori cause a large share of lymphatic filariasis in South and Southeast Asia, and the standard circulating-filarial-antigen test does not see them. The alternative — antibody tests — cannot distinguish current from past infection. Brugia Test Plus detects IgG4 antibodies against two Brugia antigens simultaneously, was independently evaluated in Malaysia, the United States and Indonesia, and performed reproducibly in high-temperature, high-humidity field conditions. It is an example of a diagnostic built to fill a specific hole in the elimination toolkit rather than a general improvement.
Sources: Drugs & Diagnostics for Tropical Diseases — lymphatic filariasis <https://www.ddtd.org/lymphatic-filariasis>; WHO — lymphatic filariasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/lymphatic-filariasis>; FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>

### Buruli ulcer LAMP test
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/buruli-ulcer-lamp/
TL;DR: An isothermal molecular test for Mycobacterium ulcerans that gives a result in about 30 minutes near the point of care.
Summary: Buruli ulcer is confirmed by PCR for the IS2404 sequence, but PCR needs a reference laboratory that most endemic districts do not have, so diagnosis is often made on appearance and made late. Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) for M. ulcerans runs at a single temperature and can be done with simple equipment near the patient; the FIND Test Directory lists an open-source M. ulcerans LAMP kit that takes about 30 minutes at true point of care. It is still research-use only, but it points at the test the field has asked for: molecular accuracy without a reference laboratory, so treatment can start before the lesion extends.
Sources: FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>; WHO — Buruli ulcer (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/buruli-ulcer>

### Card agglutination test for trypanosomiasis (CATT)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/catt/
TL;DR: A field test for Gambiense sleeping sickness that detects antibodies and has driven decades of active screening.
Summary: CATT mixes the patient's blood with stained trypanosomes that agglutinate in the presence of specific antibodies. It made mass screening for sleeping sickness possible in remote settings without a laboratory. Because it detects antibodies it cannot distinguish current from past infection, so a positive CATT is followed by parasite confirmation. It works for Gambiense disease but not for Rhodesiense, for which there is no comparable rapid test.
Sources: WHO — human African trypanosomiasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/trypanosomiasis-human-african-(sleeping-sickness)>; WHO — human African trypanosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/human-african-trypanosomiasis>; FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>

### Cartridge-based molecular tests
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/gene-cartridge-test/
TL;DR: Self-contained cartridges that run a molecular test at the point of care, like the platforms built for tuberculosis.
Summary: Cartridge platforms automate sample preparation and DNA amplification inside a sealed disposable, so a molecular result can be obtained with minimal training outside a laboratory. The tuberculosis cartridge is the best-known example and has been adapted for NTDs and for detecting drug resistance. For NTD programmes their promise is sensitive diagnosis where it is needed; their obstacles are cost per test, the need for a powered instrument, and the fact that different diseases need different cartridges.
Sources: FIND — cartridge-based molecular diagnostics <https://www.finddx.org/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>; FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>

### Chagas serology and blood-donor screening
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/chagas-serology/
TL;DR: Two different antibody tests are needed to confirm Chagas disease, and every blood donor in affected regions should be screened.
Summary: Because Trypanosoma cruzi is hard to see in blood during chronic infection, diagnosis rests on detecting antibodies — and because those tests are imperfect, WHO requires two different serological methods to agree before calling a case confirmed. The same tests screen blood donors and pregnant women, which is how transfusion transmission has been largely stopped in Latin America and how congenital cases are found. Screening is also required in non-endemic countries receiving migrants from affected regions.
Sources: WHO — Chagas disease <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/chagas-disease-(american-trypanosomiasis)>; WHO — Chagas disease (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/chagas-disease>; FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>

### Chikungunya RT-PCR
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/chikungunya-rt-pcr/
TL;DR: Molecular detection of chikungunya virus RNA in the first week of illness, before antibodies appear.
Summary: RT-PCR detects chikungunya virus RNA in blood during the first week of illness — the window before IgM appears — and is the test of choice for early confirmation. Its importance is not only diagnostic: chikungunya, dengue and Zika co-circulate, look alike clinically and share a vector, but they need different management. Dengue requires fluid monitoring and a watch for shock, and NSAIDs must be avoided until dengue is excluded because of bleeding risk, so a test that distinguishes them changes what a clinician does.
Sources: WHO — chikungunya (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/chikungunya>; PAHO — chikungunya <https://www.paho.org/en/topics/chikungunya>; FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>

### Chikungunya serology
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/chikungunya-serology/
TL;DR: Antibody tests for chikungunya, mostly as part of multiplex fever panels rather than as a dedicated rapid test.
Summary: Chikungunya is confirmed by RT-PCR in the first week and by antibody testing afterwards, but the FIND Test Directory shows how thin the dedicated serology market is: most chikungunya antibody tests are components of multiplex fever panels rather than standalone rapid tests. That matters for programmes, because it means chikungunya is usually diagnosed only where a multiplex panel or a reference laboratory is available, and otherwise is missed in the dengue-like fevers that fill clinics. Where serology is used, IgM rises in the first week and IgG indicates past infection; cross-reactivity with other alphaviruses and with dengue complicates interpretation.
Sources: FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>; WHO — chikungunya (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/chikungunya>

### Cysticercosis serology (EITB and rT24H)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/cysticercosis-serology/
TL;DR: Antibody tests that confirm exposure to the pork tapeworm, used alongside imaging to diagnose brain cysts.
Summary: Diagnosing neurocysticercosis combines imaging with serology. The enzyme-linked immunoelectrotransfer blot (EITB, also called the LLGP-EITB) detects antibodies against specific Taenia solium glycoproteins and is highly specific; the rT24H assay uses a recombinant antigen and is easier to standardise and deploy. Both indicate exposure rather than active disease and cannot show whether a lesion in the brain is alive, so they are read together with CT or MRI and with the clinical picture. Detecting the tapeworm carrier — the person actually shedding eggs — is a separate and harder problem, relying on stool examination or coproantigen tests that are insensitive at low burdens. A point-of-care test for active infection and for the carrier state is one of the field's clearest unmet needs.
Sources: WHO — taeniasis/cysticercosis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/taeniasis-cysticercosis>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>; FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>

### Dengue molecular tests
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/dengue-molecular/
TL;DR: Nucleic-acid tests for dengue, including a portable platform that gives a result in about 35 minutes near the point of care.
Summary: Dengue molecular testing is used for early diagnosis, for serotype surveillance and for blood-donor screening, where the NS1 antigen and antibody tests perform poorly. The FIND Test Directory distinguishes three uses: portable polymerase-chain-reaction platforms such as Truenat that bring molecular testing near the point of care; laboratory kits for reference and surveillance laboratories; and highly sensitive assays for plasma donation screening. Serotyping matters because a second infection with a different serotype carries a higher risk of severe dengue, and because the circulating serotype drives outbreak risk. This is a case where the same disease needs quite different tests depending on whether the question is clinical care, surveillance or blood safety.
Sources: FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>; WHO — dengue and severe dengue (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/dengue-and-severe-dengue>

### Dengue NS1 rapid test
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/dengue-ns1-rdt/
TL;DR: A lateral-flow test for the dengue NS1 antigen that gives a result in minutes during the first days of illness.
Summary: The NS1 antigen test detects a non-structural dengue protein in blood during the first days of illness, when virus is present and before antibodies appear. It is fast, needs no laboratory, and is the mainstay of point-of-care dengue diagnosis during outbreaks — but it is less sensitive after about day five, and it cannot reliably separate the four serotypes or distinguish a primary from a secondary infection, so RT-PCR remains the confirmatory test. Its value is practical: it lets a clinician classify a febrile patient and start the fluid monitoring that severe dengue requires.
Sources: WHO — dengue and severe dengue (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/dengue-and-severe-dengue>; PAHO — dengue <https://www.paho.org/en/topics/dengue>; FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>

### Direct agglutination test (DAT)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/direct-agglutination-test/
TL;DR: A laboratory test for visceral leishmaniasis that detects antibodies by visible clumping, and works well in East Africa.
Summary: DAT mixes the patient's serum with stained Leishmania promastigotes; antibodies cause the parasites to clump, which is read visually. It is inexpensive and works better than rK39 in East Africa, where that strip underperforms. Its drawbacks are that it needs a cold chain, a laboratory and overnight incubation, so it is not a village-level test.
Sources: WHO — leishmaniasis diagnostics <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leishmaniasis>; WHO — leishmaniasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leishmaniasis>; FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>

### Dual rapid diagnostic test for yaws
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/yaws-dual-rdt/
TL;DR: A rapid test that combines a treponemal and a non-treponemal line, helping separate active yaws from past infection — and from syphilis.
Summary: Yaws is caused by Treponema pallidum subsp. pertenue, and the antibodies it provokes cross-react with those of venereal syphilis, so a simple treponemal test cannot tell the two apart or distinguish active infection from old. Dual rapid diagnostic tests address this by combining a treponemal line, which detects any exposure, with a non-treponemal line, which is more indicative of active infection — the same approach used in syphilis screening. WHO and partners have also developed a target product profile for a second, harder test: one that detects the macrolide resistance mutations that would compromise azithromycin, the antibiotic the entire eradication strategy depends on. That resistance test does not yet exist as a field product.
Sources: Diagnostics to support the eradication of yaws — target product profiles <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9473620/>; WHO — yaws (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/yaws>; FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>

### Ebola RT-PCR
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/ebola-rt-pcr/
TL;DR: The molecular test that confirms Ebola infection, and the test on which outbreak response depends.
Summary: Ebola is confirmed by detecting viral RNA in blood, usually by RT-PCR. Because viral load rises over the first days of illness, an early negative test does not exclude infection, and patients are retested. The test defines who is a case, who must be isolated and whose contacts must be traced — so its availability, speed and accuracy shape the entire response. During outbreaks, laboratory capacity is often established from scratch, frequently in tents near treatment centres.
Sources: WHO — Ebola disease (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/ebola-disease>; WHO — Ebola disease (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/ebola-disease>; FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>

### Filarial test strip (FTS)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/filarial-test-strip/
TL;DR: A rapid antigen test for lymphatic filariasis that falls after the worms die, so it can show whether transmission has actually stopped.
Summary: The FTS is a lateral-flow test for circulating filarial antigen from adult Wuchereria bancrofti worms. Its crucial advantage over antibody tests is behaviour after cure: because it detects the parasite's own antigen rather than the host's antibody response, it falls when the adult worms die, so a negative result means something about the present rather than the past. It is used for mapping, for assessing the impact of mass treatment and for post-validation surveillance, and it is far more practical than night blood films, which require a sample taken when microfilariae are in the bloodstream. It does not detect Brugia species, which is why a brugian test was developed separately.
Sources: WHO — lymphatic filariasis diagnostics <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/lymphatic-filariasis>; WHO — lymphatic filariasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/lymphatic-filariasis>; FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>

### Formol-ether concentration
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/formol-ether-concentration/
TL;DR: A stool concentration technique that makes light worm infections easier to see under a microscope.
Summary: The formol-ether (or formol-ethyl acetate) concentration method separates parasite eggs and cysts from stool debris by centrifugation, so more of the sample can be examined and light infections that a direct smear would miss become visible. It is a workhorse of diagnostic parasitology, though it is less quantitative than Kato-Katz for measuring infection intensity.
Sources: WHO — soil-transmitted helminth diagnostics <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/soil-transmitted-helminth-infections>; WHO — soil-transmitted helminthiases (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/soil-transmitted-helminthiases>; FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>

### Fungal biomarkers for mycetoma
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/mycetoma-biomarker/
TL;DR: Blood tests for fungal β-glucan that can support the diagnosis of eumycetoma where culture and imaging are unavailable.
Summary: Mycetoma is diagnosed from the grains discharged by the lesion, by culture and by imaging, all of which are scarce where the disease is endemic. The FIND Test Directory lists two regulatory-achieved β-glucan assays — Fungitell and a FUJIFILM Wako test — that detect a fungal cell-wall component in blood and are used in invasive fungal disease. They cannot distinguish the fungus that causes eumycetoma from other fungi, and they are laboratory tests, but they offer a signal that a fungal rather than a bacterial cause is at work, which is the decision that determines whether a patient needs azole antifungals or antibiotics. It is a good example of a test that is not specific to the NTD but can still change its management.
Sources: FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>; WHO — mycetoma (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mycetoma>

### Kato-Katz stool smear
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/kato-katz/
TL;DR: The standard microscope method for counting worm eggs in stool — cheap, quantitative and the benchmark for schistosomiasis and gut worms.
Summary: A measured sample of stool is sieved, pressed through a template onto a slide and examined under a microscope; the egg count is expressed as eggs per gram. It needs only a microscope and a trained technician, which is why it is used almost everywhere. Its weaknesses are declining sensitivity when infection intensity is low — exactly the situation at the end of an elimination campaign — and the need for a fresh sample examined within about an hour for hookworm.
Sources: WHO — schistosomiasis diagnostics <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/schistosomiasis>; WHO — schistosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/schistosomiasis>; FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>

### LAMP assay for yaws and azithromycin resistance
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/lamp-yaws/
TL;DR: A field-usable molecular test for treponemes and the resistance mutations, trialled in West Africa.
Summary: Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) can detect Treponema DNA without the laboratory infrastructure PCR needs. The EDCTP is supporting evaluation of a LAMP assay that detects both treponemes and azithromycin-resistance mutations in Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana — the piece that would let programmes monitor for resistance in the field rather than discovering it after a campaign fails. It answers one of the two diagnostic target product profiles WHO set for yaws eradication: the resistance test.
Sources: WHO — yaws (fact sheet, LAMP evaluation) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/yaws>

### Leprosy skin test antigens (MLSA-LAM and MLCwA)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/leprosy-skin-test-antigens/
TL;DR: Candidate skin-test antigens designed to reveal leprosy infection before disease appears — a missing piece of leprosy diagnosis.
Summary: Diagnosing leprosy still depends on a trained examiner finding skin patches with sensory loss and thickened nerves; there is no simple test that shows who is infected but not yet ill, which is exactly what control needs to interrupt transmission. New leprosy skin-test antigens — MLSA-LAM and MLCwA — were evaluated in a Phase 1 study sponsored by NIAID, the first step toward a test of infection rather than disease. They matter because a positive skin test given to contacts could target prophylaxis and surveillance the way the tuberculin test targeted preventive treatment for tuberculosis; leprosy has never had that tool, and the poor performance of antibody tests in paucibacillary disease is why it is needed.
Sources: NIAID — new leprosy skin test antigens, Phase 1 (NCT01920750) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01920750>; WHO — leprosy (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leprosy>

### Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/molecular-lamp/
TL;DR: A DNA test that runs at one warm temperature, bringing molecular detection closer to the field.
Summary: LAMP amplifies parasite DNA at a constant temperature of around 60–65°C without a thermal cycler, so it can run on a simple heat block. For schistosomiasis and other NTDs it offers much greater sensitivity than microscopy for light infections, which matters for verifying elimination. Its practical limits are reagent cost, strict contamination control, and the need for reliable electricity and a cold chain for some reagents.
Sources: FIND — molecular diagnostics <https://www.finddx.org/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>; FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>

### Malaria rapid diagnostic test
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/malaria-rdt/
TL;DR: A finger-prick strip that detects malaria parasite antigens in fifteen minutes, and that made test-and-treat possible in villages.
Summary: Malaria rapid diagnostic tests detect parasite proteins — usually histidine-rich protein 2 for Plasmodium falciparum — on a lateral-flow strip, with no microscope or electricity. They transformed malaria care by allowing a health worker to confirm infection before treatment, which is what makes test-and-treat policy workable and prevents the blind prescribing that drives resistance. Their weaknesses are heat sensitivity, the deletion of the hrp2 gene in some parasite populations that makes them falsely negative, and their inability to quantify parasite density — which microscopy and molecular testing still provide.
Sources: WHO — malaria (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/malaria>; WHO — guidelines for malaria <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/guidelines-for-malaria>; FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>

### Mini-FLOTAC
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/mini-flotac/
TL;DR: A stool concentration technique more sensitive than the standard smear for counting worm eggs, and easier to standardise.
Summary: Mini-FLOTAC is a flotation-based method for counting helminth eggs in stool. It detects more low-intensity infections than the standard Kato-Katz smear and uses a closed, standardised apparatus that reduces operator variability and exposure to faecal material. As soil-transmitted helminth programmes move from controlling disease to eliminating it as a public health problem, they need diagnostics sensitive enough to certify that moderate and heavy infections have fallen below the target threshold, and Mini-FLOTAC is one of the practical options — alongside molecular methods, which are more sensitive still but cost more.
Sources: WHO — soil-transmitted helminth infections <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/soil-transmitted-helminth-infections>; WHO — soil-transmitted helminthiases (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/soil-transmitted-helminthiases>; FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>

### Mobile 'suitcase laboratory' (recombinase polymerase amplification)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/buruli-rpa-suitcase/
TL;DR: A field laboratory in two Pelican cases that brings M. ulcerans confirmation to the community.
Summary: Molecular PCR is the gold standard for confirming Buruli ulcer, but it usually happens in a reference laboratory far from where patients live, so results arrive too late to guide early treatment. This platform, developed and deployed in Ghana by the Kumasi Centre for Collaborative Research, packs a recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) assay for M. ulcerans into two portable cases (each about 56 × 45.5 × 26.5 cm). Evaluated in the field, it showed that clinically suspected lesions can be confirmed close to the community, cutting the delay and the cost of transporting samples to a distant laboratory. It directly addresses WHO's research priority for a rapid, field-usable diagnostic — though RPA still needs a cold chain for reagents and trained staff, and it is a confirmation test rather than the simple point-of-care device the target product profile envisages.
Sources: Mobile suitcase laboratory for Buruli ulcer diagnosis in Ghana (PLoS NTD 2026) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42081507>

### Molecular tuberculosis test with rifampicin resistance (Xpert MTB/RIF)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/xpert-mtb-rif/
TL;DR: A cartridge-based test that detects tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance in under two hours, from a sputum sample.
Summary: This test automated molecular tuberculosis diagnosis and made resistance detection routine. It amplifies the bacterium's DNA and simultaneously identifies mutations in the rifampicin-resistance gene, so a patient can be started on the right treatment the same day rather than waiting weeks for culture. It is also a marker for multidrug resistance, since rifampicin resistance usually accompanies isoniazid resistance. Its limits are cost, the need for an instrument and power, and lower sensitivity in people with HIV and in children, who produce fewer bacteria in sputum.
Sources: WHO — tuberculosis (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/tuberculosis>; WHO — tuberculosis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/tuberculosis>; FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>

### Multiplex fever panels
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/multiplex-arbovirus-pcr/
TL;DR: Cartridge-based molecular panels that test one sample for dengue, chikungunya, Zika, malaria and haemorrhagic fevers at once.
Summary: Dengue, chikungunya, Zika, malaria, leptospirosis and the viral haemorrhagic fevers present with the same fever and are hard to tell apart clinically, but they need different management. Multiplex molecular panels answer that problem directly: a single cartridge or open-source kit tests one blood sample for many pathogens at once, and several are regulatory-achieved at or near the point of care with results in about an hour. The FIND Test Directory lists both fully automated cartridge platforms (BioFire) and open-source RT-qPCR panels (TRUPCR, Bosphore), which differ sharply in cost, instrument needs and suitability for district laboratories. They are the clearest example of a diagnostics trend that changes NTD outbreak response: the arboviruses and haemorrhagic fevers are tested together rather than one at a time.
Sources: FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>; WHO — dengue and severe dengue (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/dengue-and-severe-dengue>

### Mycolactone detection
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/mycolactone-detection/
TL;DR: A test for the toxin the Buruli ulcer bacterium produces, which could allow diagnosis at a district clinic rather than a reference laboratory.
Summary: Mycobacterium ulcerans causes disease entirely through mycolactone, its toxin, so detecting the toxin is a direct way to diagnose the infection. Fluorescent thin-layer chromatography has been used to detect it, and a mycolactone-specific lateral flow assay was reported in a 2024 case study. The value is practical: PCR requires a reference laboratory and a sample transport chain, whereas a toxin test could be done where the patient presents, allowing treatment to start before the lesion extends. A rapid test at primary-health-care level is one of WHO's stated research priorities for Buruli ulcer — WHO's 2022 target product profile sets out the performance such a test would need — precisely because late diagnosis is the main driver of disability.
Sources: WHO — Target product profile for a rapid Buruli ulcer test (2022) <https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/353982>; WHO — Buruli ulcer research priorities <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases/buruli-ulcer/research-priorities>; J Clin Tuberc Other Mycobact Dis — mycolactone lateral flow assay case report (2024) <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jctube.2024.100469>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>; FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>

### OraQuick Ebola rapid antigen test
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/ebola-rdt-oraquick/
TL;DR: The first licensed rapid test for Ebola — a 30-minute strip for blood and cadaveric oral fluid, with a 2026 successor covering all ebolaviruses.
Summary: Until 2019 every Ebola diagnosis required a molecular laboratory, which outbreaks often had to build from tents. The OraQuick Ebola Rapid Antigen Test, a lateral-flow strip detecting Ebolavirus-genus antigens in fingerstick or venous blood and in cadaveric oral fluid, became the first Ebola rapid test the US FDA allowed to market (De Novo, 10 October 2019). Results are presumptive and must be confirmed by RT-PCR; clinical sensitivity was 84% in patient blood and 97% in cadaveric buccal swabs, with specificity above 98%. Its genus-level design — it does not distinguish Zaire, Sudan, Bundibugyo or Taï Forest viruses — became an asset in 2026: the OraQuick Ebola 2.0 version, under emergency authorisation, explicitly covers all four, and was positioned for the Bundibugyo response alongside Cepheid's donated Xpert Hemorrhagic Fever cartridges on the existing GeneXpert footprint.
Sources: FDA — first rapid Ebola test allowed to market (Oct 2019) <https://www.fda.gov/emergency-preparedness-and-response/mcm-issues/ebola>; Wang et al. — clinical evaluation of OraQuick Ebola (2023) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36851550>

### Ov16 rapid test for onchocerciasis
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/onchocerciasis-ov16-rdt/
TL;DR: An antibody rapid test for onchocerciasis that detects exposure to the parasite without a skin snip, and now comes in a combined onchocerciasis/lymphatic filariasis format.
Summary: Diagnosing onchocerciasis historically meant a skin snip — a bloodless biopsy incubated in saline and examined under a microscope — which is invasive, insensitive in low-intensity infection and unpopular with communities. The Ov16 antibody test detects IgG4 against the parasite's Ov16 antigen from a finger-prick blood sample and is now used for mapping, stopping-MDA decisions and post-elimination surveillance. The FIND Test Directory also lists a combined onchocerciasis/lymphatic filariasis IgG4 biplex test, which matters where both infections circulate and programmes are integrating. Because antibody tests cannot separate past from current infection, they are surveillance rather than diagnostic tools.
Sources: FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>; WHO — onchocerciasis (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/onchocerciasis>

### Photographic and AI-assisted trachoma grading
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/ai-trachoma-grading/
TL;DR: Standardising the eye exam with photographs and machine learning, so prevalence surveys agree.
Summary: Trachoma is graded by eye using the WHO simplified system, which makes survey results depend on how human graders differ. Photographic grading — with images later read centrally, increasingly by machine-learning models — reduces that variability and allows remote quality assurance. As prevalence falls and surveys decide whether a district can stop mass treatment, the reliability of grading becomes the whole ballgame; AI-assisted grading is how programmes are trying to make the measurements trustworthy and cheaper to repeat.
Sources: Training data recorders for high-quality trachoma photographs (Am J Trop Med Hyg 2026) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42447856>

### Point-of-care circulating cathodic antigen (POC-CCA)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/point-of-care-cca/
TL;DR: A urine strip test for schistosomiasis that gives a result in minutes, without a microscope or a stool sample.
Summary: POC-CCA is a lateral-flow test that detects an antigen released by adult schistosomes into urine. It requires no electricity, no microscope and no stool, and it detects most moderate and heavy Schistosoma mansoni infections well. It tends to read positive for weeks after successful treatment, which limits its use for test-of-cure, and its sensitivity for light S. haematobium infection is debated. It remains a research-grade product rather than a WHO-prequalified device.
Sources: WHO — schistosomiasis diagnostics <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/schistosomiasis>; WHO — schistosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/schistosomiasis>; FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>

### Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/molecular-pcr/
TL;DR: The most sensitive way to detect a parasite's DNA, used for confirmation, low-intensity infection and surveillance.
Summary: PCR copies a specific DNA sequence many times over so that even trace amounts can be detected, and quantitative PCR can estimate the parasite load. It is valuable exactly where microscopy fails: light infections, post-treatment monitoring and pooled surveillance samples. In most NTD settings it is a laboratory and reference test, limited by cost, equipment, clean facilities and trained staff — the constraints that field-friendly molecular platforms are trying to remove.
Sources: WHO — molecular diagnostics for NTDs <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>; FIND — Test Directory Explorer <https://finddx.shinyapps.io/testdirexplorer_beta/>

### Prepatent guinea-worm serology (TRX/DUF148, experimental)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/prepatent-guinea-worm-serology/
TL;DR: The first blood test that can detect guinea worm in a dog months before the worm emerges — the missing tool for finding infections while they can still be contained.
Summary: Guinea worm has always been diagnosed by seeing the worm emerge, 10–14 months after infection — by which time containment is a race. Two recombinant antigens, TRX (thioredoxin-like) and DUF148, detect prepatent D. medinensis infection in dog serum by indirect ELISA: in a 2025 evaluation DUF148 reached 76.6% sensitivity, 85.2% specificity and an AUC of 0.87, with an antigen cocktail at 78.7% sensitivity. Cross-reactivity with other filarial sera (Brugia, Onchocerca lupi, shelter-dog panels) remains the limitation, and DUF148-derived peptides are being tested to fix it. A 2024 modelling study showed that even an imperfect prepatent test would pay off if used to target tethering, which is exactly the use WHO's 2024 target product profile specifies. The test is research-use-only, not a product.
Sources: Hakimi et al. — TRX and DUF148 for prepatent detection in dogs (2025) <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12678139>; WHO — target product profile: prepatent D. medinensis infection in animals (2024) <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240090804>; Smalley et al. — potential impact of a prepatent test in dogs (2024) <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11066357>

### Rapid diagnostic test for onchocerciasis elimination (in development)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/diagnostics/oncho-rapid-diagnostic-test/
