It is the most powerful and the most contested new vector-control idea: it could suppress a species durably without chemicals, but it is self-propagating, essentially irreversible once released, and raises governance questions that have kept field releases to contained trials so far.
Sources: WHO — guidance framework for gene drive <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241511988>; WHO — Global vector control response <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241512978>

### Genomic surveillance
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/genomic-surveillance/
TL;DR: Sequencing pathogen DNA to track strains, spot drug resistance and follow how a parasite moves between places.
Summary: Whole-genome sequencing of parasites and vectors reveals drug-resistance mutations, whether an infection is locally transmitted or imported, and how strains spread. For NTD elimination the last question is critical: proving that a residual case was imported rather than locally acquired is what allows a country to claim elimination. Genomic capacity is growing in endemic countries, but it is unevenly distributed and sample logistics remain hard.
Sources: WHO — genomic surveillance for NTDs <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Hookworm vaccine candidates
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/hookworm-vaccine-candidates/
TL;DR: Experimental vaccines that aim to stop hookworm by blocking the parasite's feeding and development, not just killing adults already in the gut.
Summary: Repeated deworming treats hookworm but does not prevent reinfection, so a vaccine that reduces the intensity of infection would add something drugs cannot. Candidates target enzymes the worm needs to feed and digest blood, and have been taken through early clinical trials. The challenge is that hookworm has evolved to modulate the human immune response, so inducing durable protection is hard.
Sources: WHO — soil-transmitted helminths <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/soil-transmitted-helminth-infections>; WHO — soil-transmitted helminthiases (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/soil-transmitted-helminthiases>

### Indoor residual spraying
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/indoor-residual-spraying/
TL;DR: Spraying the inside walls of houses with long-lasting insecticide so that resting vectors pick up a lethal dose.
Summary: Indoor residual spraying targets mosquitoes and bugs that rest on interior walls after feeding, such as the Anopheles and Culex mosquitoes and triatomine bugs. It can suppress transmission in a whole community from a small amount of insecticide. Its weaknesses are cost and logistics, community acceptance, and resistance — and for Chagas disease it must be combined with housing improvement, because the bugs live in the wall cracks themselves.
Sources: WHO — vector control <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241512978>

### Insecticide-treated nets
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/insecticide-treated-nets/
TL;DR: Bed nets treated with insecticide that kill or repel night-biting mosquitoes and vectors.
Summary: Insecticide-treated nets protect the sleeper and, at high community coverage, kill enough mosquitoes to reduce transmission for everyone. They are the single most effective vector-control tool for night-biting mosquitoes, which makes them central to lymphatic filariasis control, and they have some effect on sandflies. They do not work against day-biting Aedes aegypti, the dengue vector, which is a fundamental limitation.
Sources: WHO — vector control <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241512978>

### Ivermectin mass drug administration for scabies
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/scabies-mda/
TL;DR: Treating a whole community at once with oral ivermectin, which is the only approach that stops scabies coming straight back.
Summary: Scabies recurs relentlessly if only the patient is treated, because the mite is reintroduced by everyone around them. Mass drug administration — treating an entire community with oral ivermectin, with topical permethrin for those who cannot take it — reduces both scabies and impetigo prevalence, and has been delivered at scale in Pacific island countries and Ethiopia. A cluster-randomised trial suggested that a single round may be as effective as two, which matters for cost and logistics, and WHO's 2024 consultation on combining NTD mass-treatment regimens raised the prospect of giving scabies treatment alongside lymphatic filariasis or trachoma campaigns using the same delivery machinery.
Sources: WHO — scabies <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/scabies>; WHO — scabies (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/scabies>

### Lateral-flow assays
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/lateral-flow-assays/
TL;DR: The paper-strip format behind rapid tests — a drop of sample flows along a membrane and a coloured line gives the answer.
Summary: Lateral-flow assays are the technology behind most point-of-care NTD tests: rK39 for visceral leishmaniasis, POC-CCA for schistosomiasis, and antibody strips for filariasis and exposure mapping. They are cheap, need no equipment and are easy to use. Their limits are well known — antibody strips stay positive after cure, heat degrades some reagents, and sensitivity for light infection is often inadequate for elimination programmes.
Sources: FIND — rapid diagnostic tests <https://www.finddx.org/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Leishmaniasis vaccine candidates
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/leishmaniasis-vaccine-candidates/
TL;DR: Vaccines for leishmaniasis, motivated by the fact that people who recover from the skin form are protected for life.
Summary: Recovery from cutaneous leishmaniasis confers lasting immunity, which is the strongest evidence that a vaccine is possible. Candidates include defined recombinant antigens, live attenuated parasites and viral-vectored vaccines. Progress has been slow because leishmaniasis is a family of diseases, immunity is species-specific, and there is no commercial market to fund late-stage trials.
Sources: WHO — leishmaniasis vaccine development <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leishmaniasis>; WHO — leishmaniasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leishmaniasis>

### LepVax — a leprosy-specific vaccine
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/lepvax/
TL;DR: The first vaccine developed specifically for leprosy, and the only leprosy vaccine in clinical development — in Phase Ib trials led from Brazil.
Summary: LepVax, developed by American Leprosy Missions, is a defined recombinant protein vaccine designed around antigens of Mycobacterium leprae — the first candidate built for leprosy itself rather than borrowed from tuberculosis, and the only leprosy vaccine in clinical development. A Phase Ib trial is being run by Fiocruz in Brazil, evaluating the vaccine for both prevention among contacts and adjunctive treatment. For a disease whose control still depends on finding cases late and giving chemoprophylaxis to their contacts, a vaccine would change the arithmetic — and its existence answers the standing claim that leprosy is simply too slow and too poorly understood to vaccinate against. The field's own strategy documents treat an effective vaccine as the missing tool for interrupting transmission.
Sources: G-FINDER 2024 — pipeline update: LepVax Phase Ib <https://cdn.impactglobalhealth.org/media/G-FINDER%202024_Full%20report.pdf>; WHO — leprosy (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leprosy>

### Malaria vaccines (RTS,S and R21)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/malaria-vaccines/
TL;DR: Two recommended vaccines against falciparum malaria, ending decades in which a malaria vaccine was assumed impossible.
Summary: For decades a malaria vaccine was considered impractical because the parasite has thousands of antigens and a complex life cycle, and the first candidate took thirty years to develop. WHO recommended RTS,S/AS01 in 2021 for children in moderate-to-high transmission settings, and R21/Matrix-M in 2023. Both target the circumsporozoite protein and reduce clinical malaria by roughly a third to a half, which is not enough to eliminate malaria but is enough to save tens of thousands of lives a year — and R21 can be produced at much greater scale and lower cost.
Sources: WHO — malaria (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/malaria>; WHO — malaria (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/malaria>

### Mass drug administration
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/mass-drug-administration/
TL;DR: Treating an entire community on a schedule with safe donated medicines, whether or not each person is tested, to break transmission.
Summary: Mass drug administration is the delivery model behind preventive chemotherapy for five NTDs. Rather than test everyone, programmes treat the whole eligible population in a district once or twice a year with medicines that are safe enough to give without diagnosis. Repeated rounds reduce the reservoir of infection until transmission can no longer sustain itself. What determines success is coverage — WHO's target is at least 65% of the eligible population — and whether the same people are reached year after year.
Sources: WHO — preventive chemotherapy <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Mobile health and digital surveillance
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/mhealth-surveillance/
TL;DR: Using phones and simple digital tools to report cases, track campaigns and map where disease is still occurring.
Summary: Mobile reporting lets community workers and clinics submit case data, campaign coverage and geolocated outbreak signals without a computer or a paper trail. For NTDs it supports case-based surveillance for guinea worm, coverage monitoring for mass administration, and rapid reporting of dengue or cholera-like clusters. Its value is timeliness and granularity; its risks are data quality, fragmentation across systems, and the digital divide in the poorest districts.
Sources: WHO — NTD surveillance <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Mosquito autodissemination stations
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/mosquito-autodissemination/
TL;DR: Stations that let mosquitoes pick up a larvicide and spread it to breeding sites themselves.
Summary: Autodissemination is vector control that exploits mosquito behaviour: stations attract adult mosquitoes, which pick up a transferable larvicide (such as pyriproxyfen) or an entomopathogenic fungus (such as Beauveria bassiana), then carry it to the hidden breeding sites where they lay eggs, contaminating the water and killing larvae. Because it uses the insects to deliver the control agent, it can reach cryptic breeding sites that spraying and source-reduction miss. A 2026 randomised controlled field trial in urban Melbourne suppressed Aedes notoscriptus and reduced modelled Buruli ulcer risk — the first controlled evidence that vector control can lower human Buruli ulcer risk. Its transferability to African freshwater transmission cycles, where the vectors and reservoirs are less certain, is unproven.
Sources: Autodissemination stations reduce Buruli ulcer risk (Nat Microbiol 2026) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42661072>

### Nanobody-based recombinant antivenoms
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/nanobody-antivenoms/
TL;DR: Tiny engineered antibodies produced in cells, not horses — an oligoclonal mix that protected mice against cobra venoms.
Summary: Nanobodies are single-domain antibody fragments, small and stable, that can be engineered and produced recombinantly rather than harvested from immunised animals. Because venom is a cocktail of toxins, an effective product must be oligoclonal — several nanobodies combined. In 2026 an oligoclonal nanobody-based recombinant antivenom protected mice challenged with venoms from cobras and king cobras, a proof-of-concept for the engineered-antibody route. The advantages are consistency, scalability and no animal immunisation; the challenges are covering every important toxin, and the economics of a market made up of poor rural communities — which is why WHO's 2026 novel-treatment target product profiles matter.
Sources: Oligoclonal nanobody antivenom protects mice (Sci Transl Med 2026) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42715346>; Engineering antivenom: research progress and future directions (2026) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42644833>

### Onchocerciasis vaccine candidates
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/onchocerciasis-vaccine-candidates/
TL;DR: Experimental vaccines for river blindness, explored because drug treatment is lifelong and cannot kill adult worms.
Summary: Mass ivermectin controls river blindness but does not cure it: adult worms live for years and treatment must continue until they die naturally. A vaccine would change that equation, and candidates have been tested in animal models with some reduction in worm burden. The field is early, and the regulatory and trial infrastructure for a vaccine in a disease already 'under control' is a significant obstacle.
Sources: WHO — onchocerciasis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/onchocerciasis>; WHO — onchocerciasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/onchocerciasis>

### One Health NTD integration
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/one-health-ntd-integration/
TL;DR: Running human and animal health programmes together, because several NTDs live in animals and cannot be stopped by treating people alone.
Summary: For zoonotic NTDs — rabies, echinococcosis, taeniasis/cysticercosis, foodborne trematodiases — human treatment cannot eliminate the infection while the animal or environmental reservoir remains. One Health integration means vaccinating dogs to stop rabies, deworming dogs and controlling slaughter to stop hydatid disease, and managing livestock and aquaculture to stop foodborne trematodes. The obstacle is institutional: ministries of health and agriculture rarely plan together, and funding is siloed.
Sources: WHO — One Health <https://www.who.int/health-topics/one-health>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Open-science drug discovery
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/open-science-drug-discovery/
TL;DR: Developing medicines for diseases with no market by publishing everything and collaborating across institutions, as DNDi does.
Summary: Because an NTD medicine cannot earn a commercial return, the product development partnership model develops it on public and philanthropic funding and then ensures affordable access. DNDi's portfolio — fexinidazole and acoziborole for sleeping sickness, benznidazole access for Chagas, DNDi-0690 and emodepside — shows the model can deliver approved drugs. Open science, virtual screening consortia and data sharing further reduce the cost of each candidate.
Sources: DNDi — portfolio <https://dndi.org/portfolio/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### PAIR (puncture, aspiration, injection, reaspiration)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/pair/
TL;DR: A minimally invasive technique that collapses a hydatid cyst through a needle instead of open surgery.
Summary: PAIR is a procedure for treating echinococcal liver cysts without open surgery: the cyst is punctured under ultrasound guidance, its fluid aspirated, a scolicidal solution injected to kill the contents, and the fluid reaspirated. It is used alongside albendazole, which is given before and after to reduce the risk of the procedure spreading infection, and it shortens hospital stays and recovery compared with surgery. It is not suitable for every cyst — the WHO classification determines whether a cyst is better observed, drained this way, or operated on — which is why standardised imaging and staging matter so much.
Sources: WHO — echinococcosis <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/echinococcosis>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Protein structure prediction (AlphaFold)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/alphafold-structure-prediction/
TL;DR: Software that predicts the 3D shape of a protein from its sequence, giving drug hunters a structure for targets that were never crystallised.
Summary: Determining a protein's structure experimentally can take years. Deep-learning prediction, led by AlphaFold and open databases such as the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, produces a usable model from sequence alone. For NTD drug discovery this is transformative: many parasite proteins have no experimental structure, and a predicted model is enough to start virtual screening and to understand where a drug could bind.
Sources: AlphaFold Protein Structure Database <https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Rabies vaccination and dog vaccination
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/rabies-vaccination/
TL;DR: Vaccinating dogs breaks human rabies at its source, and vaccinating people after a bite prevents the disease entirely.
Summary: Human rabies can be eliminated by vaccinating the dogs that cause almost all cases — a strategy proven in the Americas and pursued in Africa and Asia — combined with prompt post-exposure prophylaxis for anyone bitten. Progress is limited by the cost and access of human vaccine and immunoglobulin, and by the logistics of reaching enough dogs to maintain herd immunity.
Sources: WHO — rabies <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/rabies>; WHO — rabies (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/rabies>

### Recombinant and next-generation antivenoms
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/recombinant-antivenoms/
TL;DR: Antivenoms made from engineered antibodies instead of horse serum, aiming to end the shortages and reactions of today's products.
Summary: Conventional antivenoms are made by immunising horses, which yields variable products, requires a cold chain, and carries a risk of allergic reactions. Recombinant antivenoms built from human monoclonal antibodies could be produced consistently, at scale, without animals. The scientific challenge is that venom is a cocktail of many toxins, so a product must combine antibodies against several of them — a hard engineering problem now being pursued with support from WHO's snakebite programme.
Sources: WHO — snakebite envenoming <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/snakebite-envenoming>; WHO — snakebite envenoming strategy <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241515993>

### Recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/molecular-rpa/
TL;DR: An isothermal molecular test that can confirm an infection in a field laboratory without a thermal cycler.
Summary: Recombinase polymerase amplification is an isothermal nucleic-acid amplification method: instead of cycling temperatures as PCR does, it uses recombinase enzymes to open the DNA and a polymerase to extend primers at a single constant temperature, so it needs only a simple heat block rather than a thermal cycler. That makes it suitable for a portable, field-deployable laboratory — the basis of the mobile 'suitcase laboratory' that detects M. ulcerans in Ghana. RPA is fast (typically under 30 minutes), but like other molecular tests it needs cold-chain reagents, trained staff and quality control, so it is a step toward point-of-care confirmation rather than a fully self-contained device.
Sources: Mobile suitcase laboratory for Buruli ulcer diagnosis in Ghana (PLoS NTD 2026) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42081507>

### Ring vaccination
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/ring-vaccination/
TL;DR: Vaccinating the contacts of every case and their contacts — a strategy borrowed from smallpox that ends Ebola outbreaks.
Summary: Ring vaccination means finding every new case, identifying everyone they had contact with, and vaccinating those contacts and their contacts. It creates a protective ring that stops the virus reaching anyone beyond it, and it works even without vaccinating a whole population. The strategy was inherited from smallpox eradication and proved itself against Ebola in the 2015 Guinea trial and then in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It depends entirely on contact tracing, which is why surveillance and community trust are the determinants of whether it succeeds.
Sources: WHO — Ebola disease (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/ebola-disease>; WHO — Ebola disease (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/ebola-disease>

### Seasonal malaria chemoprevention
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/seasonal-malaria-chemoprevention/
TL;DR: Giving antimalarials to children during the rainy season, when transmission peaks, whether or not they are infected.
Summary: Seasonal malaria chemoprevention delivers monthly antimalarial treatment to children under five during the transmission season in the Sahel and sub-Saharan belt, where malaria is intensely seasonal. It does not treat existing infection as a diagnosis would; it keeps children protected through the months when they are most at risk, in the same way that preventive chemotherapy works for NTDs. It prevents a large share of cases and deaths, and it is one of the clearest examples of the NTD and malaria worlds using the same delivery logic — which is why integrating the two campaigns is now being explored.
Sources: WHO — malaria (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/malaria>; WHO — malaria (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/malaria>

### Snail control
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/snail-control/
TL;DR: Reducing the freshwater snails that schistosomes need to complete their life cycle, using molluscicides or habitat management.
Summary: Because each schistosome species needs a specific snail host, removing the snail breaks the cycle before the parasite can infect anyone. Methods include the molluscicide niclosamide, clearing vegetation and modifying irrigation and water infrastructure, and biological approaches. Snail control was central to early schistosomiasis programmes, fell out of favour when praziquantel arrived, and is now being reconsidered for elimination, where stopping transmission needs more than treating people.
Sources: WHO — schistosomiasis control <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/schistosomiasis>; WHO — schistosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/schistosomiasis>

### Sterile insect technique
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/sterile-insect-technique/
TL;DR: Releasing large numbers of sterilised male insects so that wild females mate with them and produce no offspring.
Summary: The sterile insect technique irradiates mass-reared male insects so they are sterile but still compete for mates; repeated releases collapse the wild population. It is species-specific, leaves no chemical residue and has been used for decades against agricultural pests and against the tsetse fly. For mosquitoes the practical barriers are the need to rear and sex-sort millions of insects and the fact that releases must be sustained.
Sources: WHO — sterile insect technique <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241512978>

### The SAFE strategy for trachoma
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/safe-strategy/
TL;DR: Surgery, antibiotics, facial cleanliness and environmental improvement — a four-part strategy matched to each stage of trachoma.
Summary: SAFE is the intervention model that has taken trachoma to the edge of elimination. Surgery treats trichiasis in people whose eyelids have already turned inward; antibiotics — mass azithromycin — reduce the community pool of infection; facial cleanliness reduces transmission between children; and environmental improvement, meaning water supply and latrines, attacks the conditions that allow the infection to spread, including the flies that feed on eye and nose discharge. It is the clearest example in the NTD field of pairing a medical intervention with a development one, and the reason WHO now recommends combining preventive chemotherapy with water and sanitation rather than running them as separate programmes.
Sources: WHO — trachoma <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/trachoma>; WHO — trachoma (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/trachoma>

### Tiny targets for tsetse control
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/tiny-targets/
TL;DR: Low-cost insecticide-treated cloth targets that kill tsetse flies and cost a fraction of traps, letting programmes cover far more ground.
Summary: Tiny targets are small, insecticide-treated cloth panels that attract and kill tsetse flies. Their significance is cost and coverage: because they are cheap and simple, programmes can deploy them densely across the riverine and lakeside habitats where tsetse concentrate, suppressing a local fly population enough to interrupt transmission of human African trypanosomiasis without treating everyone at risk. They are typically deployed alongside case-finding, and they make vector control feasible in the remote, sparsely served areas where sleeping sickness persists.
Sources: WHO — human African trypanosomiasis <https://www.who.int/health-topics/human-african-trypanosomiasis>

### Total community treatment (TCT) for yaws
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/total-community-treatment/
TL;DR: Treating every person in an endemic community with one dose of azithromycin, repeated until yaws transmission stops.
Summary: The Morges strategy for yaws eradication runs on total community treatment: mass administration of a single oral dose of azithromycin to everyone in an affected community, followed by total targeted treatment — cases and their contacts only — as prevalence falls. TCT is feasible because azithromycin is a one-dose cure that needs no injection and can be given by a community health worker, which is what distinguishes it from the injectable penicillin campaigns that nearly eradicated yaws in the 1950s. Its vulnerability is the same as its strength: the entire strategy depends on one antibiotic, and azithromycin-resistant yaws has already emerged in Papua New Guinea.
Sources: WHO — supporting countries to implement the yaws eradication strategy <https://www.who.int/activities/supporting-endemic-countries-to-implement-yaws-eradication-strategy>; WHO — yaws (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/yaws>

### Triple-drug therapy (IDA)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/triple-drug-therapy-ida/
TL;DR: Ivermectin, DEC and albendazole given together in one dose, which clears filarial worms faster than two-drug regimens and can shorten elimination programmes.
Summary: IDA is a single co-administered dose of ivermectin, diethylcarbamazine and albendazole for lymphatic filariasis. Compared with the earlier two-drug regimens it removes microfilariae from the blood far more completely after the first round, and modelling and field experience suggest it can cut the number of annual treatment rounds a country needs to reach the elimination threshold. WHO recommended it in 2017, and programmes including Kenya's have used it to accelerate. Its limitation is geographic: DEC is unsafe in people who also carry onchocerciasis or Loa loa, so IDA cannot be used where those infections co-circulate — which excludes much of West and Central Africa.
Sources: WHO — lymphatic filariasis treatment <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/lymphatic-filariasis>; WHO — lymphatic filariasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/lymphatic-filariasis>

### Tsetse traps and targets
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/tsetse-traps/
TL;DR: Cloth traps and insecticide-treated targets that attract and kill tsetse flies, cutting sleeping-sickness transmission.
Summary: Tsetse flies are attracted to certain colours and shapes that mimic a host; traps and insecticide-treated targets exploit this to kill them with minimal insecticide. Because tsetse reproduce slowly and live in defined habitats, targeted trapping can suppress a local population enough to interrupt transmission even without treating people. It was one of the tools that pushed Gambiense sleeping sickness to its lowest recorded levels.
Sources: WHO — human African trypanosomiasis control <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/trypanosomiasis-human-african-(sleeping-sickness)>; WHO — human African trypanosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/human-african-trypanosomiasis>

### TSOL18 pig vaccine (Cysvax)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/tsol18-vaccine/
TL;DR: A vaccine that stops pigs developing tapeworm cysts, breaking the cycle that gives people neurocysticercosis.
Summary: TSOL18 is a recombinant vaccine against Taenia solium in pigs. Because pigs are the intermediate host, preventing cysts in pigs removes the step that lets people acquire the adult tapeworm — and therefore removes the tapeworm carriers who contaminate the environment with the eggs that cause brain cysts. It is produced commercially as Cysvax by Indian Immunologicals and is named by WHO among the specific animal-side control measures for the disease. The vaccine prevents new cysts but does not clear existing ones, so it is used with oxfendazole, which kills established cysts; a trial in Uganda found that three-monthly vaccination combined with oxfendazole eliminated transmission by pigs.
Sources: WHO — Taenia solium prevention through animals, One Health approach <https://www.who.int/activities/promoting-prevention-and-control-of-taenia-solium-infection-through-animals-with-the-one-health-approach/promoting-prevention-and-control-of-taenia-solium-infection-through-animals-with-the-one-health-approach>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Tuberculosis preventive treatment
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/tb-preventive-treatment/
TL;DR: Treating people with latent tuberculosis infection before they become ill — the closest thing to a strategy for eliminating the disease.
Summary: A quarter of the world is estimated to carry latent tuberculosis, and roughly a tenth of those will develop active disease. Preventive treatment gives one or two drugs for one to six months to people at highest risk — household contacts, young children, and people with HIV — to stop that happening. WHO recommends a cascade of testing and treatment, and shorter rifamycin-based regimens have made it far more practical than the old nine-month isoniazid course. It is the intervention that most resembles an NTD elimination strategy: treating people who are not ill to stop transmission and disease later.
Sources: WHO — tuberculosis (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/tuberculosis>; WHO — tuberculosis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/tuberculosis>

### Vector surveillance
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/vector-surveillance/
TL;DR: Systematically catching, counting and testing vectors to know where and when the risk is highest.
Summary: Vector surveillance includes trapping adult mosquitoes and flies, sampling larvae, mapping breeding sites, and testing captured insects for infection. It tells a programme whether transmission is rising or falling, where to spray, and whether resistance is appearing. It is chronically underfunded relative to treatment, yet without it vector control is blind — spraying the wrong place or continuing a failing insecticide.
Sources: WHO — Global vector control response <https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241512978>

### WASH interventions
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/wash-interventions/
TL;DR: Clean water, safe toilets and hygiene promotion that stop the worms, flukes and bacteria spread through water, stool and soil.
Summary: For schistosomiasis, soil-transmitted helminths, trachoma, dracunculiasis and the foodborne trematodiases, drugs reduce the burden but cannot stop reinfection where sanitation and water are unsafe. WASH interventions — safe water supply, latrines, handwashing, shoe-wearing and safe food handling — attack the transmission route itself. WHO now recommends integrating WASH with preventive chemotherapy and vector control, since the two together can achieve what neither can alone.
Sources: WHO — WASH and NTDs <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>

### Wolbachia mosquito method
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/wolbachia-method/
TL;DR: Releasing mosquitoes that carry a common bacterium so that they can no longer transmit dengue, chikungunya or Zika — and so that their offspring cannot either.
Summary: The World Mosquito Program's method infects Aedes aegypti with the wMel strain of Wolbachia, a bacterium that blocks dengue, chikungunya and Zika viruses from replicating well inside the mosquito. Because Wolbachia is passed from mother to eggs, the bacterium spreads through the wild mosquito population and persists without repeated releases — a replacement rather than a suppression strategy. The evidence base is strong: a cluster-randomised trial in Yogyakarta found 77% fewer dengue cases and 86% fewer hospitalisations, and city-scale deployments in Brazil and Colombia have reported reductions of 60–90%, sustained through the severe 2024 outbreak. By 2025 the programme reported 16.1 million people protected across fifteen countries, with an estimated 1.5 million cases prevented. It is not a vaccine and does not stop every case, but no other dengue intervention has produced reductions this large and durable at city scale.
Sources: World Mosquito Program <https://www.worldmosquitoprogram.org/>; AWED trial results (NEJM) <https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2030243>; WHO — dengue and severe dengue (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/dengue-and-severe-dengue>

### Xenomonitoring
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/technologies/xenomonitoring/
TL;DR: Testing the vectors themselves for infection, rather than testing people, to see whether transmission is still happening.
Summary: Xenomonitoring examines trapped mosquitoes, flies, bugs or snails for the parasite's DNA. Because many NTD infections are asymptomatic, human surveys can miss low-level transmission; testing the vector detects it directly. It has become a key tool for verifying whether lymphatic filariasis and onchocerciasis transmission has actually stopped, which is exactly the question elimination programmes must answer.
Sources: WHO — xenomonitoring for NTD elimination <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>


## Trials

### ACOZI-KIDS: single-dose acoziborole in children 1–14
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/acozi-kids/
TL;DR: The trial closing the paediatric gap — crushed single-dose tablets for the youngest patients.
Summary: ACOZI-KIDS (EDCTP2-funded, DRC and Guinea) tested single-dose acoziborole in 35 children aged 1 to 14 across all weight bands, with crushed tablets for those unable to swallow whole ones. Recruitment completed in March 2025 and 12-month follow-up in 2026. Children were historically the most neglected subgroup — adult tablets, no dosing data — so this small trial carries the registration for everyone the pivotal adult study left out.
Sources: EDCTP — single-dose treatment approved (Mar 2026) <https://www.global-health-edctp3.europa.eu/news-and-events/news/new-single-dose-oral-treatment-approved-fight-sleeping-sickness-2026-03-18_en>

### Acoziborole single-dose trial for sleeping sickness
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/acoziborole-hat/
TL;DR: A trial of a single oral dose of acoziborole that reported cure rates above 95% in Gambiense sleeping sickness, including late-stage disease.
Summary: DNDi and partners tested acoziborole, a benzoxaborole, as a single oral treatment for Gambiense human African trypanosomiasis in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Guinea. Reported cure rates were very high across both early and late-stage disease without the lumbar puncture staging that older treatments required. If registration follows, treatment could be given in a village clinic with one tablet — no hospital, no infusions, no cold chain.
Sources: DNDi — acoziborole for sleeping sickness <https://dndi.org/diseases/sleeping-sickness/>; DNDi — DRC approves acoziborole <https://dndi.org/press-releases/2026/drc-approves-use-acoziborole-breakthrough-one-day-oral-treatment-against-sleeping-sickness/>; WHO — human African trypanosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/human-african-trypanosomiasis>; ACOZIBOROLE pivotal study (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05256017) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05256017>

### AI-based early detection of skin NTDs (including podoconiosis)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/podoconiosis-ai-detection/
TL;DR: A trial using AI-assisted image recognition to find skin NTDs early — an attempt to give podoconiosis the screening tool it has never had.
Summary: Podoconiosis is diagnosed clinically, by a trained eye recognising the characteristic below-knee swelling in someone with a history of barefoot farming on irritant soil. In the rural highland communities where it occurs, that trained eye is scarce, so cases are found late, when swelling is established and irreversible. This trial (NCT07506967) tests early detection and AI-based management of skin-related neglected tropical diseases, using image recognition to help community-level workers identify cases sooner. If it works, it addresses the disease's central operational gap — early detection — and does so through a tool that can sit in a phone rather than a clinic. It also reflects the wider movement toward integrating skin NTDs into one screening pathway.
Sources: Early detection and AI-based management of skin NTDs (NCT07506967) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07506967>; Bushara et al. — modelling approaches for predicting skin NTD distribution (PLoS NTD 2026) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40220765/>

### Albendazole for early alveolar echinococcosis (Kyrgyzstan)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/ae-kyrgyzstan-albendazole-trial/
TL;DR: The first randomised trial asking whether early alveolar lesions need albendazole at all — or whether some resolve on their own.
Summary: Ultrasound surveillance in Osh province, Kyrgyzstan, found a new focus of alveolar echinococcosis with about 6% prevalence, most lesions small. Because albendazole is parasitostatic rather than curative and is otherwise given for life, the trial randomised 194 people with early-stage lesions to albendazole (400 mg twice daily) or placebo, watching lesions by imaging and serology: if treated lesions regress while untreated ones progress, early treatment is justified; if both regress, many early cases resolve spontaneously and lifelong treatment is overtreatment. Run 2017–2023 and posted to ClinicalTrials.gov in September 2025, it is the rare prospective experiment in a field that runs almost entirely on retrospective series — and its design concedes the central uncertainty of alveolar disease management.
Sources: Albendazole for early alveolar echinococcosis (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07182305) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07182305>; WHO — echinococcosis (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/echinococcosis>

### Albendazole vs tribendimidine vs praziquantel for clonorchiasis (Guangxi)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/tribendimidine-clonorchiasis-guangxi/
TL;DR: The head-to-head Phase 4 that could give liver flukes their second drug.
Summary: This recruiting Phase 4 trial in Guangxi randomises clonorchiasis patients to albendazole, single-dose tribendimidine (400 mg), or praziquantel. It follows the Laos Phase 2 non-inferiority result (tribendimidine vs praziquantel for O. viverrini) and the network meta-analysis (~90% cure for single-dose tribendimidine in opisthorchiasis): a positive readout makes tribendimidine — already registered in China for soil-transmitted helminths — the first credible alternative to praziquantel monotherapy for liver flukes.
Sources: Guangxi clonorchiasis trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07074444) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07074444>

### AN2-502998 Phase II proof-of-concept in chronic Chagas
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/an2-502998-phase2/
TL;DR: The planned late-2026 efficacy trial of the CPSF3 inhibitor that cured naturally infected primates.
Summary: Following 100% parasite elimination in naturally infected primates and a clean Phase 1 profile at clinically attainable exposures (June 2026), AN2 Therapeutics with DNDi plans a Phase II proof-of-concept study of oral AN2-502998 in chronic Chagas disease starting late in 2026, run on DNDi's Latin American trial network with possible US and Australian sites. The goal is the first demonstration of a well-tolerated, short-course parasitological cure in chronic Chagas — the milestone fexinidazole and the azoles never reached.
Sources: AN2 — enabling data (June 2026) <https://investor.an2therapeutics.com/news-releases/news-release-details/an2-therapeutics-reports-positive-enabling-data-supporting>; DNDi — AN2 collaboration (July 2025) <https://dndi.org/press-releases/2025/an2-therapeutics-and-dndi-collaborate-on-clinical-development-of-promising-new-oral-compound-to-treat-chronic-chagas-disease>

### Arpraziquantel for preschool-aged children (introduction study)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/arpraziquantel-introduction/
TL;DR: A large implementation study introducing the child-friendly arpraziquantel tablet to preschool-aged children in Kenya, Côte d'Ivoire and Uganda.
Summary: Arpraziquantel is the paediatric formulation of praziquantel for children from 3 months to 6 years, a group that carries a heavy schistosome burden but was almost never treated because the standard tablet is large and bitter. After a positive European Medicines Agency opinion in 2023 and WHO prequalification in 2024, this small-scale public-health intervention study introduced the dispersible tablet to preschool-aged children in Kenya, Côte d'Ivoire and Uganda, aiming to enrol 18,500 children and working out how to deliver it through routine services. It is the delivery counterpart to the efficacy trial, and a model for turning a new formulation into programme practice.
Sources: Arpraziquantel introduction study (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06698510) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06698510>; WHO — schistosomiasis (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/schistosomiasis>

### Autodissemination stations to cut Buruli ulcer risk (Melbourne trial)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/buruli-autodissemination-trial/
TL;DR: The first randomised evidence that controlling mosquitoes lowers human Buruli ulcer risk.
Summary: In urban Victoria the Buruli ulcer bacterium is transmitted in part by Aedes notoscriptus mosquitoes, which can pick M. ulcerans up from possum excreta and contaminate people they bite. This randomised controlled field trial, run in an endemic part of Melbourne between January and March 2024, deployed autodissemination mosquito-control stations containing pyriproxyfen (an insect growth regulator/larvicide) and the entomopathogenic fungus Beauveria bassiana: six geographic areas each received 100 stations for eight weeks, six control areas received none. The stations suppressed Aedes notoscriptus populations and reduced modelled Buruli ulcer risk, giving the first controlled evidence that vector control can lower human risk rather than merely correlating with it. Whether an equivalent intervention can be designed for African freshwater transmission cycles — where the vectors and reservoirs are different and largely unknown — remains the open question.
Sources: Autodissemination stations reduce Buruli ulcer risk (Nat Microbiol 2026) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42661072>

### AWED: Wolbachia to eliminate dengue
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/awed-wolbachia/
TL;DR: The gold-standard randomised trial that showed Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes cut dengue by 77% and hospitalisations by 86%.
Summary: The AWED trial was a cluster-randomised controlled trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, in which Wolbachia-infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes were released across part of the city and dengue incidence compared with untreated areas. It found a 77% reduction in virologically-confirmed symptomatic dengue and an 86% reduction in hospitalisations — a result of a size and rigour rarely seen for a vector-control intervention. The trial is the foundation of the World Mosquito Program's case for scaling the method, and subsequent city-scale deployments in Brazil and Colombia have reported reductions of similar magnitude. Yogyakarta recorded only 67 dengue cases in 2023, a fraction of its historical burden.
Sources: Efficacy of Wolbachia-infected mosquito deployments (NEJM) <https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2030243>; WHO — dengue and severe dengue (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/dengue-and-severe-dengue>

### Azithromycin for yaws eradication
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/yaws-azithromycin/
TL;DR: The trial showing a single oral dose of azithromycin cures yaws as well as an injected penicillin, enabling mass eradication.
Summary: A landmark study in Papua New Guinea found that a single oral dose of azithromycin was non-inferior to injected benzathine penicillin for curing yaws. That result made community-wide mass treatment possible, and in 2012 WHO launched the Morges strategy to eradicate yaws. Progress has been slowed by resurges and by the difficulty of reaching the last affected communities.
Sources: WHO — yaws eradication <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/yaws>; WHO — yaws (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/yaws>; Three-round azithromycin MDA for yaws (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03490123) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03490123>; Azithromycin versus benzathine penicillin for yaws (PACTR201306000520103) <https://pactr.samrc.ac.za/TrialDisplay.aspx?TrialID=520>

### Azithromycin mass treatment for trachoma
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/trachoma-azithromycin/
TL;DR: Trials showing that single-dose azithromycin reduces the eye infection that causes trachoma, forming the 'A' in the SAFE strategy.
Summary: Randomised trials in Tanzania and elsewhere showed that single-dose oral azithromycin dramatically reduced the prevalence of the chlamydial eye infection that leads to trachoma, compared with topical treatment. This established the 'A' in WHO's SAFE strategy (surgery, antibiotics, facial cleanliness, environmental improvement) and turned trachoma from an intractable cause of blindness into an elimination target.
Sources: WHO — trachoma elimination <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/trachoma>; WHO — trachoma (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/trachoma>; Enhancing the A in SAFE (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05634759) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05634759>

### BDQ4LEP: bedaquiline for multibacillary leprosy (Mali)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/bdq4lep-leprosy/
TL;DR: A PACTR-registered pilot trial of bedaquiline added to standard multidrug therapy for multibacillary leprosy in Mali.
Summary: Leprosy treatment has been unchanged for decades, and shorter or stronger regimens are needed. BDQ4LEP is a pilot clinical trial run in Mali and registered retrospectively in the Pan African Clinical Trials Registry in 2024, testing bedaquiline — already used for drug-resistant tuberculosis — in people with multibacillary leprosy. It complements the BE-PEOPLE prophylaxis trials by testing bedaquiline as treatment, and it is one of the relatively few leprosy treatment trials registered in an African registry.
Sources: BDQ4LEP (PACTR202408643515316) <https://pactr.samrc.ac.za/TrialDisplay.aspx?TrialID=31799>; WHO — leprosy (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/leprosy>

### BE-PEOPLE: bedaquiline as leprosy prophylaxis
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/be-people-leprosy/
TL;DR: A trial testing whether bedaquiline, with its very long half-life, protects contacts of leprosy patients better than a single dose of rifampicin.
Summary: BE-PEOPLE tests bedaquiline as post-exposure prophylaxis for leprosy contacts. The rationale is pharmacological: bedaquiline has a half-life of around five and a half months and greater activity against Mycobacterium leprae than rifampicin, so a single dose might protect for far longer. If it works, it would be the first genuinely new preventive agent for leprosy since single-dose rifampicin, and could be particularly valuable in high-burden settings where repeated contact screening is impractical.
Sources: Leprosy research updates — bedaquiline prophylaxis <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12010777/>; WHO — leprosy (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leprosy>; BE-PEOPLE Phase 2 (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05406479) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05406479>; BE-PEOPLE Phase 3 (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05597280) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05597280>

### BENEFIT: benznidazole in chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/benefit-chagas/
TL;DR: The largest Chagas treatment trial, which found that benznidazole cleared the parasite but did not clearly improve heart outcomes.
Summary: BENEFIT randomised 2,854 patients with established Chagas cardiomyopathy at 49 centres in Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia and El Salvador to benznidazole (5 mg/kg/day for 40–80 days) or placebo, with a mean follow-up of 5.4 years. The drug reduced detectable parasite DNA, but it did not significantly reduce cardiac clinical deterioration on the composite outcome (death, resuscitated arrest, sustained ventricular tachycardia, pacemaker/ICD insertion, transplantation, new heart failure, stroke or thromboembolism). The result reshaped the field: it showed that treating late-stage disease is not the same as curing it, and that the priority is finding patients earlier and developing better drugs.
Sources: Randomised trial of benznidazole for chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy (NEJM 2015) <https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1507574>; WHO — Chagas disease treatment <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/chagas-disease-(american-trypanosomiasis)>; WHO — Chagas disease (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/chagas-disease>; BENEFIT trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00123916) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00123916>

### BENLATINO: short benznidazole regimens in Bolivia and Colombia
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/benlatino-short-bzn/
TL;DR: A Fiocruz-sponsored phase 3 non-inferiority trial of two short benznidazole regimens in indeterminate and mild-cardiac disease.
Summary: BENLATINO is a double-blind, phase 3 randomised, multicentre non-inferiority trial sponsored by Fiocruz, evaluating two short benznidazole regimens against the standard course in adults with chronic indeterminate or mild-cardiac Chagas disease in Bolivia and Colombia. Together with NuestroBen it forms the phase 3 confirmation of the MULTIBENZ short-course signal.
Sources: BENLATINO trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06339710) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06339710>

### BLMs4BU: beta-lactam regimen to shorten Buruli ulcer therapy
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/blms4bu/
TL;DR: A Phase 2 trial testing whether adding amoxicillin-clavulanate lets the 8-week cure finish in 4 weeks.
Summary: Buruli ulcer is cured by eight weeks of rifampicin plus clarithromycin, but eight weeks is a long journey for patients far from a clinic. BLMs4BU is a Phase 2 randomised trial testing whether adding amoxicillin-clavulanate — a beta-lactam/beta-lactamase-inhibitor combination long used for other infections — to the standard rifampicin–clarithromycin pair allows the course to be cut to four weeks without loss of cure. It is led by the Fundación Agencia Aragonesa para la Investigación y Desarrollo (ARAID) with the University of Zaragoza and, critically, the Université d'Abomey-Calavi in Benin, where patients are enrolled; the Raoul Follereau Foundation, Anesvad, the Instituto de Salud Carlos III, the Tres Cantos Open Lab Foundation and GSK collaborate. Beginning in December 2021 with a target of 140 participants and a primary completion in 2026, it is the most advanced alternative to the telacebec route for shortening treatment — and unlike a new molecule, it uses two off-patent antibiotics already on the shelf.
Sources: ClinicalTrials.gov — BLMs4BU (NCT05169554) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05169554>

### BRAVIO: varespladib for snakebite envenoming
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/varespladib-snakebite/
TL;DR: A Phase 2 trial of varespladib, a drug designed to work against many snake venoms, added to standard antivenom.
Summary: Antivenom is specific to the snake that bit the patient, expensive, and often unavailable — so a drug that works across many venoms would be transformative. Varespladib inhibits secretory phospholipase A2, a toxin family present in many snake venoms. The BRAVIO trial, sponsored by Ophirex, gave intravenous then oral varespladib alongside standard of care to people bitten by vipers and elapids, measuring severity and recovery. It completed in November 2024; a broad-spectrum snakebite drug remains one of the field's highest priorities.
Sources: BRAVIO varespladib trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05717062) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05717062>; WHO — snakebite envenoming (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/snakebite-envenoming>

### Butantan-DV single-dose dengue vaccine trial
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/butantan-dv-dengue/
TL;DR: A Brazilian single-dose dengue vaccine trial reporting strong efficacy across serotypes and age groups.
Summary: Butantan-DV is a single-dose, live-attenuated tetravalent dengue vaccine developed in Brazil. A large randomised trial reported substantial efficacy against symptomatic dengue across all four serotypes and in both younger and older participants, with a good safety profile. A single-dose vaccine removes a major logistical obstacle for mass programmes in middle-income countries.
Sources: WHO — dengue vaccines <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/dengue-and-severe-dengue>; WHO — dengue and severe dengue (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/dengue-and-severe-dengue>; Butantan-DV Phase 3 (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02406729) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02406729>

### CHAGASAZOL: posaconazole vs benznidazole for chronic Chagas
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/chagasazol-posaconazole/
TL;DR: The randomised trial that showed the antifungal posaconazole fails where benznidazole works.
Summary: CHAGASAZOL randomised adults with chronic T. cruzi infection to low- or high-dose posaconazole vs benznidazole. Posaconazole showed initial antitrypanosomal activity, but significantly more posaconazole patients had treatment failure (positive RT-PCR on follow-up) than benznidazole patients. Together with the E1224/ravuconazole failure, it closed the repurposed-azole chapter and explains why the CYP51 record must be read as a caution, not a promise.
Sources: Posaconazole vs benznidazole for chronic Chagas (NEJM 2014) <https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1313122>

### Cipargamin plus GanLum Phase 2
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/cipargamin-ganlum-ph2/
TL;DR: Pairing the fastest killer with the newest drug for a simplified regimen.
Summary: Novartis/MMV test cipargamin (PfATP4) with GanLum (NCT05750628) to see whether the combination permits simplified dosing while protecting both mechanisms from resistance. Phase 2 oral and IV-severe studies of cipargamin are complete; this pairing decides its field future.
Sources: MMV — GanLum plus cipargamin pipeline <https://www.mmv.org/mmv-pipeline-antimalarial-drugs/ganaplacide-lumefantrinecipargamin>

### Combined oral ivermectin and permethrin for severe scabies (NEJM 2026)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/severe-scabies-ivermectin-permethrin/
TL;DR: The randomised trial showing combination therapy cures severe scabies better than permethrin alone — and that raising the ivermectin dose does not.
Summary: This randomised trial compared standard-dose oral ivermectin plus 5% permethrin cream against topical permethrin alone in patients with severe scabies — abundant mites, often crusted, in whom the probability of cure was previously uncertain and no randomised data existed. The combination improved cure, establishing that the win comes from pairing the two drugs rather than from escalating ivermectin; a parallel analysis confirmed that higher ivermectin doses do not improve outcomes. It gives the field its first randomised evidence for how to treat the most infectious, life-threatening form.
Sources: Combined oral ivermectin and 5% permethrin for severe scabies (NEJM 2026) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42090793>

### Dimeticone versus sodium carbonate for tungiasis
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/tungiasis-dimeticone-trial/
TL;DR: A randomised comparison of two field treatments for embedded jigger fleas.
Summary: Tungiasis treatment is unglamorous and evidence is thin. This randomised, parallel-group study in Kenya compared dimeticone oils with sodium carbonate solution for embedded Tunga penetrans, one of the few head-to-head tests of field-usable treatments for the jigger flea. It addresses a disease that disables people who walk barefoot in infested soil, where the practical question is which simple topical actually works.
Sources: Dimeticone vs sodium carbonate for tungiasis (Trop Med Health 2026) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39042700>

### DNDi-0690 for visceral leishmaniasis
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/dndi-0690-leishmaniasis/
TL;DR: A non-profit-developed oxaborole for visceral leishmaniasis — a distinct compound from the better-known LXE408, and one whose clinical development was paused.
Summary: DNDi-0690 is an oxaborole from DNDi's discovery pipeline, associated with inhibition of the parasite enzyme N-myristoyltransferase. It was developed as part of the effort to find an oral treatment that avoids the toxicity of antimonials and the logistics of infusions, and illustrates the non-profit pipeline filling a gap the market left empty. It is not the same molecule as LXE408: DNDi's leishmaniasis portfolio advanced several candidates in parallel, and by 2023 DNDi-0690 and DNDi-6148 were on hold in favour of the more promising LXE408 (a proteasome inhibitor) and DNDI-6174. Reports that conflate DNDi-0690 with LXE408 are incorrect.
Sources: DNDi — leishmaniasis portfolio <https://dndi.org/diseases/leishmaniasis/>; DNDi 2023 leishmaniasis portfolio review <https://dndi.org/news/2024/2023-rd-portfolio-in-review-leishmaniasis>; WHO — leishmaniasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/leishmaniasis>; LXE408 (DNDi-0690) Phase 2, Ethiopia (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05957978) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05957978>

### E1224 (ravuconazole prodrug) for chronic Chagas disease
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/e1224-chagas/
TL;DR: The DNDi proof-of-concept trial showing ravuconazole plus benznidazole offers no durable advantage.
Summary: E1224, the prodrug of the CYP51 inhibitor ravuconazole, was tested by DNDi in a randomised, placebo-controlled proof-of-concept trial in adults with chronic indeterminate Chagas disease, alone and with benznidazole. Parasite clearance was not sustained relative to benznidazole, confirming the CHAGASAZOL lesson for a second azole and redirecting the pipeline toward non-CYP51 mechanisms such as CPSF3 and topoisomerase II.
Sources: Benznidazole and three E1224 regimens (Lancet Infect Dis 2018) <https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laninf/article/PIIS1473-3099(23)00651-5/abstract>; DNDi — fexinidazole for Chagas <https://dndi.org/research-development/portfolio/fexinidazole-chagas/>

### Ebola ring vaccination trial (Guinea)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/ebola-ring-vaccination-trial/
TL;DR: The trial that proved a vaccine could protect the contacts of Ebola cases, and gave outbreak response its most powerful tool.
Summary: Run in Guinea during the 2014–2016 West African outbreak, this trial used ring vaccination — vaccinating the contacts and contacts-of-contacts of each new case — and was designed so that efficacy could be estimated from cases occurring before vaccination took effect. It found the rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine highly protective, with no cases among vaccinated contacts after the ten-day window. The result licensed the vaccine and established ring vaccination as the standard response to Ebola, later used at scale in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Sources: WHO — Ebola disease (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/ebola-disease>; WHO — Ebola disease (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/ebola-disease>; Ebola Vaccine Ring Vaccination Trial in Guinea (PACTR201503001057193) <https://pactr.samrc.ac.za/TrialDisplay.aspx?TrialID=1057>

### EFECAB: improving pig management to prevent epilepsy (Burkina Faso)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/efecab-burkina-faso/
TL;DR: An African trial testing whether managing pigs reduces epilepsy — linking animal husbandry directly to a child neurology outcome.
Summary: EFECAB was a community trial in Burkina Faso testing whether improved pig management and hygiene could reduce Taenia solium transmission and downstream neurocysticercosis-associated epilepsy — a disease where the outcome of interest is measured not in animals but in children's seizures. It is one of the clearest One Health trials in the field: the intervention sits with pig keeping and sanitation, and the benefit is prevented epilepsy. Its African setting matters, because most of the field's evidence has come from Latin America and Asia, and control strategies built there must be tested where the parasite's epidemiology, pig husbandry and health systems differ. It represents the shift of T. solium research into the continent that carries the growing burden.
Sources: EFECAB — improving pig management to prevent epilepsy (NCT03095339) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03095339>; WHO — taeniasis/cysticercosis (fact sheet) <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/taeniasis-cysticercosis>

### Egaten safety and outcomes in fascioliasis (Novartis, 6y+)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/egaten-fascioliasis-safety/
TL;DR: The completed Phase 4 that documented triclabendazole's real-world safety in children.
Summary: Novartis's completed Phase 4 study (NCT04230148, from 2022) evaluated safety, tolerability and clinical outcomes of Egaten (triclabendazole) in fascioliasis patients aged six and over. As the only modern company-sponsored dataset on the drug's paediatric safety profile, it underpins the donation programme's continued use while resistance work proceeds — and sets the baseline any second drug must beat.
Sources: Egaten fascioliasis study (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04230148) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04230148>

### Emodepside for onchocerciasis and soil-transmitted helminths
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/emodepside-oncho/
TL;DR: Clinical development of a veterinary dewormer as a new human treatment with a mechanism different from ivermectin.
Summary: DNDi and partners advanced emodepside into human trials for onchocerciasis and soil-transmitted helminths. Because it acts on the SLO-1 potassium channel rather than the ivermectin channel, it could be used where ivermectin is contraindicated — notably areas where Loa loa circulates and ivermectin risks severe reactions — and provides a second mechanism if resistance emerges.
Sources: DNDi — emodepside <https://dndi.org/diseases/onchocerciasis/>; WHO — onchocerciasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/onchocerciasis>; Emodepside Phase 2 (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05180461) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05180461>

### Emodepside for Strongyloides stercoralis infection (Phase 2)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/emodepside-strongyloides/
TL;DR: A Phase 2 trial of emodepside against the soil worm that deworming campaigns miss entirely.
Summary: Strongyloides stercoralis is the STH that mass deworming cannot touch: it does not respond to albendazole or mebendazole, it is invisible to the standard stool tests, and in an immunocompromised person it can multiply unchecked into a fatal hyperinfection. WHO added its control as a 2030 objective, possible because prequalified ivermectin became affordable in 2021. This Phase 2 trial tested emodepside — a depsipeptide already in development for filarial disease, acting on a different channel from ivermectin — in adults infected with Strongyloides, and completed. It matters as a second option: relying on ivermectin alone repeats the single-drug dependency that left Trichuris untreated for twenty years.
Sources: Emodepside in adults infected with Strongyloides (NCT06373835) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06373835>; WHO — guideline on public health control of human strongyloidiasis (2024) <https://www.who.int/news/item/02-08-2024-who-releases-guideline-on-public-health-control-of-human-strongyloidiasis>

### Emodepside Phase II part 2 for river blindness
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/emodepside-part2-oncho/
TL;DR: The dose-selection stage of emodepside's clinical development, after part 1 showed it works against adult as well as juvenile worms.
Summary: The final analysis of part 1 of emodepside's Phase II trial confirmed a favourable safety profile and efficacy against both juvenile and adult Onchocerca volvulus worms, meeting the criteria to proceed. Part 2 will investigate selected doses and their safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics, with recruitment planned to begin in the third quarter of 2026. The significance is the adulticidal signal: ivermectin does not reliably kill adult worms, so a drug that does would shorten the fifteen-year treatment horizon that currently defines onchocerciasis elimination.
Sources: DNDi — emodepside for river blindness <https://dndi.org/research-development/portfolio/emodepside/>; WHO — onchocerciasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/onchocerciasis>; Emodepside Phase 2 (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05180461) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05180461>

### Ervebo cross-protection ring trial for Bundibugyo virus (DRC, 2026)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/ervebo-bundibugyo-ring-trial/
TL;DR: A Phase 3 ring trial asking whether the Zaire Ebola vaccine works against Bundibugyo — the fastest route to a countermeasure the outbreak does not have.
Summary: With no licensed vaccine for Bundibugyo virus and thousands of cases accumulating, WHO's vaccine advisory group (TAG-CVP) reviewed preliminary animal data suggesting Ervebo partially cross-protects against Bundibugyo — particularly against death — and on 31 July 2026 recommended prioritising Ervebo in a randomised clinical trial rather than using it outside research. A Phase 3 ring-vaccination trial of Ervebo against Bundibugyo virus disease launched in the DRC in August 2026, alongside a post-exposure-prophylaxis medicine trial in Ituri province. WHO issued emergency guidance on Ervebo use during Bundibugyo outbreaks on 31 August 2026 and a Bundibugyo vaccine target product profile in July 2026, while CEPI funded a fifth Bundibugyo-specific candidate. Efficacy is unproven and results are months away; a Bundibugyo-specific vaccine remains the preferred option.
Sources: UN News — new Ebola vaccine trial launches in DRC (Aug 2026) <https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/08/1168072>; UN News — hopes raised over new vaccine as child deaths pass 300 (Aug 2026) <https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/08/1168100>; C&EN — Ebola vaccine enters Phase 3 trial (Aug 2026) <https://cen.acs.org/pharmaceuticals/vaccines/ebola-vaccine-trial-drc/104/web/2026/08>

### eWHORM basket trial of oxfendazole
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/ewhorm-oxfendazole/
TL;DR: An African-European partnership testing one drug against several worm infections at once, including river blindness and loiasis.
Summary: The eWHORM partnership runs a basket trial — a single protocol testing oxfendazole across multiple helminth infections simultaneously — with clinical sites in Africa. Recruitment for trichuriasis was completed in Tanzania and sites for onchocerciasis and loiasis opened, alongside a Phase IIa dose-escalation study for loiasis in Gabon. The design is a response to a practical problem in NTD research: running one trial per infection is unaffordable, and a drug that works against several worms at once is exactly what a mass-treatment programme would want.
Sources: eWHORM — African-European partnership <https://www.ewhorm.org/>; WHO — onchocerciasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/onchocerciasis>; OXF 01 oxfendazole basket trial (PACTR202412611774752) <https://pactr.samrc.ac.za/TrialDisplay.aspx?TrialID=31996>

### EYU688 (Novartis NS4B inhibitor) Phase 2
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/eyu688-novartis-ph2/
TL;DR: The live NS4B programme carrying dengue antivirals after mosnodenvir's halt.
Summary: EYU688 is a Novartis small-molecule NS4B inhibitor in an ongoing Phase 2 trial (NCT06006559) — the only industry small-molecule dengue antiviral still dosing after AT-752 and JNJ-64281802 were terminated on recruitment and deprioritisation. It targets the same replication-complex biology as mosnodenvir via a different molecule, and its readout decides whether the NS4B mechanism gets a second clinical chance.
Sources: Dengue therapeutic trials mapping review (PLoS NTD 2026) <https://journals.plos.org/plosntds/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pntd.0014382>

### Fexinidazole for chronic Chagas disease
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/fexinidazole-chagas/
TL;DR: The trial that ended fexinidazole's Chagas candidacy: tolerated by patients, but unable to eliminate the parasite.
Summary: Fexinidazole is an oral drug that transformed sleeping sickness, so testing it in chronic Chagas disease — caused by a related trypanosome — was a reasonable bet. An early Phase 2 study was encouraging enough to generate real hope, reporting high efficacy at treatment durations of less than three days, but it was interrupted for tolerability reasons. A follow-up study confirmed that the drug was well tolerated and found that it did not eliminate Trypanosoma cruzi. The negative result closed this line of work and pushed DNDi's Chagas programme toward a new candidate, with a Phase II proof-of-concept study planned to begin in Latin America in late 2026.
Sources: DNDi — fexinidazole for Chagas disease <https://dndi.org/research-development/portfolio/fexinidazole-chagas/>; WHO — Chagas disease (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/chagas-disease>; Fexinidazole dosing in chronic Chagas (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03587766) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03587766>

### Fexinidazole for sleeping sickness
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/fexinidazole-hat/
TL;DR: The trial that produced the first all-oral cure for sleeping sickness, covering both stages of Gambiense disease.
Summary: The pivotal fexinidazole study, run by DNDi with Sanofi and national programmes, showed that a 10-day oral course cured Gambiense sleeping sickness patients, including those with late-stage disease, without the need for hospital infusions. It led to approval in 2019 and to the drug's addition to the WHO essential medicines list. A follow-on study tested an adjusted regimen in patients with more severe disease.
Sources: DNDi — fexinidazole <https://dndi.org/diseases/sleeping-sickness/>; WHO — human African trypanosomiasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/human-african-trypanosomiasis>; Pivotal fexinidazole study (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01685827) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01685827>

### Field evaluation of a rapid diagnostic test for onchocerciasis elimination
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/oncho-rapid-diagnostic-trial/
TL;DR: The field study that decides whether a new rapid test can do the job skin snips and Ov-16 cannot — certify that transmission has stopped.
Summary: This study evaluates a newly developed rapid diagnostic test for onchocerciasis against the diagnostics programmes currently use, with an estimated 400 participants, sponsored by Bioaster (NCT06350851). Its importance is programme-level rather than individual: if the test is specific enough to distinguish recent infection from old exposure, it can support the stopping decisions and post-treatment surveillance that elimination verification depends on — the single hardest technical problem in the onchocerciasis endgame, and one WHO's diagnostic advisory group has flagged as a priority. A test that works in the field would also make the repeated, expensive surveys that currently rely on laboratory methods cheaper and faster.
Sources: Rapid diagnostic test for onchocerciasis elimination (NCT06350851) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06350851>

### FLAME: fluorometholone after trichiasis surgery
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/flame-trichiasis/
TL;DR: A trial of adjunctive anti-inflammatory drops to reduce trichiasis recurrence after surgery.
Summary: The FLAME trial tested whether adding the corticosteroid fluorometholone after trachomatous trichiasis surgery reduces recurrence — attacking the recurrence problem pharmacologically rather than by operating again. Because the scarring that causes in-turned lashes is an inflammatory response, damping it around the time of surgery is a plausible route to better long-term outcomes, and FLAME is one of the field's attempts to prove it.
Sources: FLAME trial references (PubMed) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=FLAME+trachomatous+trichiasis+fluorometholone>

### Flubendazole field trials in dogs, Chad (2019– )
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/flubendazole-dog-trial-chad/
TL;DR: The first randomised trials of a drug against guinea worm — in dogs, not people — testing whether flubendazole plus tethering can close the animal reservoir.
Summary: Because human guinea-worm disease has no drug and no vaccine trial is possible, the only interventional trials in the field are veterinary. The first, run in 2019 across 23 high-burden Chadian villages, randomised 600 domestic dogs to subcutaneous flubendazole or placebo; the initial dog-level analysis found no significant difference, but a 33-month village-level follow-up showed flubendazole alone cut emerging dog worms by 63% and flubendazole with proactive tethering by 83% relative to baseline. A second, larger trial ("Flubendazole 2.0") was designed specifically for the realities that undermined the first — unreliable year-round access and high dog attrition — with results reported separately. The programme has never had a therapeutic tool; if the second trial confirms the effect, dog treatment becomes one.
Sources: Cleveland et al. — flubendazole trials in ferrets and dogs in Chad (2022) <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9128682>; Dupper et al. — concurrent flubendazole and tethering in dogs (2026) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41628272>; Dupper et al. — Flubendazole 2.0 trial design (2026) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42391310>

### Fosravuconazole versus itraconazole for eumycetoma
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/fosravuconazole-mycetoma/
TL;DR: The world's first randomised clinical trial for mycetoma, run in Sudan, which found fosravuconazole safe and simpler but not more effective.
Summary: This Phase 2, randomised, double-blind, active-controlled trial at a single centre in Sudan compared two once-weekly doses of fosravuconazole with daily itraconazole, each combined with surgery at six months, in patients with moderate eumycetoma. Neither fosravuconazole dose was superior to itraconazole, and both had numerically lower efficacy. The trial nevertheless established that a rigorous randomised study is possible in one of the world's hardest settings, that once-weekly dosing is safe and tolerable, and it built the infrastructure and the international collaboration on which the next mycetoma trial will depend.
Sources: Trial results (The Lancet Infectious Diseases, 2024) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39098321/>; WHO — control of neglected tropical diseases <https://www.who.int/teams/control-of-neglected-tropical-diseases>; Fosravuconazole Phase 2 proof of concept (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03086226) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03086226>

### High-dose ivermectin for onchocerciasis
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/ivermectin-dose-oncho/
TL;DR: A trial showing that a higher dose of ivermectin kills more adult worms, strengthening the push toward elimination.
Summary: Because standard ivermectin suppresses microfilariae but does not kill adult worms efficiently, a higher-dose regimen was tested to see whether it could sterilise or kill more adults. The trial reported improved efficacy, which matters for elimination — a treatment that harms adult worms shortens the years of repeated mass administration a programme must sustain.
Sources: WHO — onchocerciasis elimination <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/onchocerciasis>; WHO — onchocerciasis (health topic) <https://www.who.int/health-topics/onchocerciasis>; Ivermectin–albendazole onchocerciasis Phase 3 (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02078024) <https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02078024>

### High-dose rifampicin plus albendazole for LF (Ghana RCT)
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/rifampicin-lf-ghana/
TL;DR: A randomised trial showing a short rifampicin course rapidly clears circulating filarial antigen.
Summary: Alexander Debrah's group at KNUST ran a randomised clinical trial of high-dose rifampicin plus albendazole in lymphatic filariasis, reporting rapid clearance of circulating filarial antigen (Pathogens, 2026). Rifampicin hits Wolbachia like doxycycline but in a far shorter, more potent course — a realistic macrofilaricidal regimen where 4–6 weeks of doxycycline is not. It is the most promising short-course adulticidal signal since oxfendazole entered Phase II.
Sources: Rifampicin plus albendazole RCT (Pathogens 2026) <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=Kutu+Debrah+rifampicin+albendazole+filarial+antigen>

### IDA (ivermectin–DEC–albendazole) for onchocerciasis
URL: https://ntd.magamios.org/trials/ida-oncho-trial/
TL;DR: A PACTR-registered African trial of the three-drug IDA regimen in people with onchocerciasis, after pre-treatment with ivermectin.
Summary: The triple-drug regimen of ivermectin, diethylcarbamazine and albendazole (IDA) is the accelerating strategy for lymphatic filariasis elimination, but it had not been safely tested in people who also carry Onchocerca volvulus, because DEC can provoke severe reactions in onchocerciasis. This trial, registered in the Pan African Clinical Trials Registry in 2019 with a target of 300 participants, gave ivermectin first to clear microfilariae and then tested IDA, measuring both safety and efficacy against adult worms — an improved macrofilaricide would be a major advance for onchocerciasis elimination.
